Swizzling permutes memory layout to avoid shared memory bank conflicts:
Bank conflict fundamentals
Shared memory on NVIDIA GPUs is organized into 32 banks of 4-byte words. Simultaneous accesses to the same bank by different threads in a warp serialize, reducing effective bandwidth by up to 32×.

Bank conflict rules

swizzling and bank conflict avoidance
Swizzling permutes memory layout to avoid shared memory bank conflicts:
Bank conflict fundamentals
Shared memory on NVIDIA GPUs is organized into 32 banks of 4-byte words. Simultaneous accesses to the same bank by different threads in a warp serialize, reducing effective bandwidth by up to 32×.

Bank conflict rules 


No conflict: All threads access different banks → 1 transaction
Broadcast: All threads access same address → 1 transaction (hardware multicast)
N-way conflict: N threads access different addresses in same bank → N transactions (serialized)
Worst case: 32-way conflict when accessing column in row-major layout



Problem: Column access in row-major layout causes bank conflicts:

__shared__ float smem[128][128];  // Row-major: smem[row][col]
float val = smem[threadIdx.x][col];  // All threads hit same bank

Why this conflicts 

Address of smem[i][col] is base + (i * 128 + col) * sizeof(float).
Bank = (address / 4) % 32 = (i * 128 + col) % 32.
When col is constant, all threads map to bank col % 32 → 32-way conflict.



Bank conflict visualization 


Shared memory organized into 32 banks (4-byte words)

Without Swizzle - Column Access (32-way conflict):
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
Threads 0-31 all read column 0:

  Thread  Row  Address        Bank                  ┌──────────────────────────┐
   T0  →  0   base + 0×128    0                     │ Bank 0: T0,T1,T2...T31   │ ← 32 accesses!
   T1  →  1   base + 1×128    0                     │        (serialized)      │
   T2  →  2   base + 2×128    0                     │                          │
  ...                                               │ Bank 1: [idle]           │
  T31  → 31   base + 31×128   0                     │ Bank 2: [idle]           │
                                                    │  ...                     │
Result: 32 transactions (1 per thread, serialized)  │ Bank 31: [idle]          │
                                                    └──────────────────────────┘

With a pedagogical XOR layout:
══════════════════════════════════════════════════
physical_col = logical_col ^ (row & 31)

  Thread  Row  Swizzle          Bank  ┌─────────────────────────┐
   T0  →  0   0 ^ (0 & 31)=0       0   │ Bank 0:  T0             │
   T1  →  1   0 ^ (1 & 31)=1       1   │ Bank 1:  T1             │
  ...                                 │  ...                    │
  T31  → 31   0 ^ (31 & 31)=31    31   │ Bank 31: T31            │
                                      └─────────────────────────┘

the store and load must use the same logical-to-physical mapping. the access is conflict-free because the $32$ lanes map bijectively to the $32$ banks for a fixed logical column.



Swizzle function design
A swizzle function S: (\text{row}, \text{col}) \to \text{address} permutes the linearized address to spread consecutive rows across different banks.
XOR-based swizzle:
S(\text{row}, \text{col}) = \text{row} \cdot W + (\text{col} \oplus f(\text{row}))
where \oplus is bitwise XOR and f is a shift/mask function.
one simple teaching layout for a 32-column float tile is:

int physical_col = logical_col ^ (row & 31);
float val = smem[row][physical_col];
production layouts must also match the tensor-core instruction’s operand layout and TMA descriptor. a bank permutation that fixes one access pattern can hurt another.
CuTe swizzle atoms
CuTe encodes swizzle patterns as layout transformations via Swizzle<B, M, S> atoms:

B: number of address bits in the XOR mask
M: number of low address bits preserved
S: displacement between the two bit fields

Column Access: All threads → Bank 0 = 32-way conflict!

With Swizzling (XOR pattern):
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ Col0  Col1  Col2  ...  Col31    │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ B0    B1    B2    ...  B31      │  ← Row 0
│ B1    B2    B3    ...  B0       │  ← Row 1 (shifted!)
│ B2    B3    B4    ...  B1       │  ← Row 2 (shifted!)
│ ...                             │
└─────────────────────────────────┘

Column Access: Threads → Different banks = Conflict-free!

Teaching function: physical_col = logical_col ^ (row & 31)



Theorem (Swizzle Conflict-Free Access).
Let a_i be the shared-memory word address requested by lane i. the access is bank-conflict-free exactly when the map
i\longmapsto a_i\bmod32
is injective over the active lanes, apart from lanes that read the same address and use broadcast.
Proof. bank assignment for a 32-bit word is its word address modulo 32. distinct residues select distinct banks; an address collision is handled as broadcast. \square

online softmax recap 

streaming the softmax keeps a running maximum m and partial sum \ell per row:
m' = \max(m, m_{\text{block}}), \qquad \ell' = e^{m - m'} \ell + e^{m_{\text{block}} - m'} \ell_{\text{block}}
and the output accumulator updates as
O' = e^{m - m'} O + e^{m_{\text{block}} - m'} \tilde O_{\text{block}}
the rescaling factors guarantee the streamed result matches the two-pass softmax. proof follows by induction on the number of processed tiles.



Theorem 1. Online Softmax Correctness Theorem 

The streaming softmax algorithm produces identical results to the standard two-pass algorithm.


Proof. By induction on the number of blocks. Base case (one block) is trivial. For inductive step, show that the correction factors exactly compensate for the difference between local and global normalization constants. The key observation is that e^{m^{(old)} - m^{(updated)}} rescales old outputs to account for the new global maximum. \square

persistent kernels
Standard kernel launch:

for (int i = 0; i < num_batches; ++i) {
    matmul_kernel<<<grid, block>>>(A[i], B[i], C[i]);
}
Problems:

Kernel launch overhead (~5-10 μs per launch)
Cold caches on each launch
No data reuse across batches

Persistent kernel:

Stage:     | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | ...
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
TMA Load:  | L0| L1| L2| L3| L4| L5| L6|
Compute:   |   | C0| C1| C2| C3| C4| C5|
Store:     |   |   | S0| S1| S2| S3| S4|

Implementation pattern:

// Producer: Load warp
for (int stage = 0; stage < num_stages; ++stage) {
    cute::copy(tma_load, gmem_tile[stage], smem_tile[stage]);
    pipeline_commit();
}
 
// Consumer: MMA warps
for (int stage = 0; stage < num_stages; ++stage) {
    pipeline_wait(stage);  // Wait for load completion
 
    wgmma::mma_async(acc, smem_A[stage], smem_B[stage]);
    wgmma::commit_group();
 
    pipeline_release(stage);  // Signal load warp
}
 
wgmma::wait_group<0>();  // Wait for all MMA completion
Synchronization primitives:

pipeline_commit(): Signal load completion
pipeline_wait(stage): Wait for specific stage
wgmma::commit_group(): Commit warpgroup MMA operations
wgmma::wait_group<N>(): Wait for N most recent wgmma operations

the pipeline can hide transfer latency when the producer stays ahead of the consumer. stage count and throughput come from the compiled kernel’s resource use and the measured trace.

exponential evaluation
softmax kernels subtract the row maximum before evaluating exponentials:
p_i=\frac{\exp(x_i-m)}{\sum_j\exp(x_j-m)},

motivation
Problem: LLM inference with KV cache:

Attention requires access to key/value cache from all previous tokens
Cache grows linearly with sequence length: O(N \cdot d \cdot L)
Monolithic allocation wastes memory (padding, fragmentation)

(Kwon et al., 2023)

Store KV cache in fixed-size pages (e.g., 16 tokens per page)
Pages allocated non-contiguously (like virtual memory)
Attention kernel reads from paged storage

Monolithic allocation wastes memory (padding, fragmentation)

(Kwon et al., 2023)

Pages allocated non-contiguously (like virtual memory)
Attention kernel reads from paged storage

Benefits:

Reduced memory fragmentation
Dynamic allocation (grow cache as needed)
Efficient batching (share pages across requests)

paged attention algorithm
Given:

Query: Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d} (current token)
Key cache: \{K_0, K_1, \ldots, K_{N-1}\} stored in pages
Value cache: \{V_0, V_1, \ldots, V_{N-1}\} stored in pages
Block table: Maps logical page index to physical page address

Compute: O = \text{softmax}(Q K^T / \sqrt{d}) V.
Algorithm:

paged attention algorithm
Given:

Query: Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d} (current token)
Key cache: \{K_0, K_1, \ldots, K_{N-1}\} stored in pages
Value cache: \{V_0, V_1, \ldots, V_{N-1}\} stored in pages
Block table: Maps logical page index to physical page address

Compute: O = \text{softmax}(Q K^T / \sqrt{d}) V.
Algorithm:

1. Initialize: max_score = -inf, sum = 0, output = 0
2. For each page p:
   a. Load page p keys into shared memory
   b. Compute scores: s_i = Q · K_i / sqrt(d)
   c. Update online softmax statistics (max, sum)
   d. Load page p values into shared memory
   e. Accumulate output with correction
3. Final rescale: output = output / sum

CuTe DSL Python examples
NVIDIA’s CuTe DSL is available as a Python library in the CUTLASS package, allowing rapid prototyping and exploration of CuTe concepts before implementing in C++. The Python API mirrors the C++ API closely, making it an excellent learning tool.
setup and basics
Install CUTLASS with Python support:

pip install nvidia-cutlass
Basic imports and tensor creation:

import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
 
 
@cute.jit
def create_tensor_from_ptr(ptr: cute.Pointer):
  # Create layout: 8×5 column-major
  layout = cute.make_layout((8, 5), stride=(1, 8))
  tensor = cute.make_tensor(ptr, layout)
  return tensor
A tensor in CuTe is mathematically defined as: T(c) = *(E + L(c)) where:

E is the engine (pointer-like object for memory access)
L is the layout (coordinate-to-offset mapping)
c is a coordinate in the logical space

layout algebra operations
coalesce
The coalesce operation simplifies a layout by flattening modes while preserving the coordinate-to-offset mapping:

@cute.jit
def coalesce_example():
  # Hierarchical layout: (2, (1, 6)) with complex strides
  layout = cute.make_layout((2, (1, 6)), stride=(1, (cutlass.Int32(6), 2)))
  result = cute.coalesce(layout)
 
  print('Original:', layout)  # ((2,(1,6)), (1,(6,2)))
  print('Coalesced:', result)  # (12, 1) - simplified to rank-1
 
  # Preserves mapping: layout(i, j, k) == result(linearized_index)
  assert layout.size() == result.size()  # Both have 12 elements
Use case: Simplifying layout expressions before performing partitioning or composition.
composition
Layout composition creates a new access pattern by chaining layouts: R(c) = A(B(c))

@cute.jit
def composition_example():
  # A: 6×2 layout with stride (8, 2)
  A = cute.make_layout((6, 2), stride=(cutlass.Int32(8), 2))
 
  # B: 4×3 layout with stride (3, 1)
  B = cute.make_layout((4, 3), stride=(3, 1))
 
  # R = A ∘ B: B's coordinates index into A's domain
  R = cute.composition(A, B)
 
  print('Layout A:', A)
  print('Layout B:', B)
  print('Composition R = A ∘ B:', R)
 
  # R selects elements from A using B's pattern
  # Example: R(1, 2) = A(B(1, 2)) = A(1*3 + 2*1) = A(5)
Use case: Implementing tiling or selecting subsets of a tensor.
logical divide (tiling)
Partition a layout into tiles of a specified shape:

@cute.jit
def logical_divide_example():
  # 64×64 column-major layout
  layout = cute.make_layout((64, 64), stride=(1, 64))
 
  # Partition into 8×8 tiles
  tiled = cute.logical_divide(layout, (8, 8))
 
  print('Original shape:', layout.shape)  # (64, 64)
  print('Tiled shape:', tiled.shape)  # ((8, 8), (8, 8))
  # Outer tuple: tile dimensions
  # Inner tuple: number of tiles per dimension
 
  # Access tile (2, 3): tiled[2, 3, :, :]
  # Access element (5, 7) within tile (2, 3): tiled[2, 3, 5, 7]
This operation is fundamental to CuTe’s hierarchical tiling model: global → block → thread.

elementwise addition kernel
Complete example demonstrating CuTe kernel authoring with proper launch pattern:

# Step 1: Define device kernel
@cute.kernel
def elementwise_add_kernel(gA: cute.Tensor, gB: cute.Tensor, gC: cute.Tensor):
  # Thread indexing
  tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
  bidx, _, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()
  bdim, _, _ = cute.arch.block_dim()
 
  thread_idx = bidx * bdim + tidx
 
  # Compute global coordinate
  m, n = gA.shape
  ni = thread_idx % n
  mi = thread_idx // n
 
  # Bounds check
  if mi < m and ni < n:
    # Load, compute, store
    a_val = gA[mi, ni]
    b_val = gB[mi, ni]
    gC[mi, ni] = a_val + b_val
 
 
# Step 2: Define host wrapper
@cute.jit
def elementwise_add_launch(mA: cute.Tensor, mB: cute.Tensor, mC: cute.Tensor):
  num_threads_per_block = 256
  m, n = mA.shape
  num_blocks = (m * n + num_threads_per_block - 1) // num_threads_per_block
 
  elementwise_add_kernel(mA, mB, mC).launch(
    grid=(num_blocks, 1, 1), block=(num_threads_per_block, 1, 1)
  )
 
 
# Step 3: Prepare and convert tensors
M, N = 1024, 1024
a = torch.randn(M, N, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(M, N, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.zeros(M, N, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float16)
 
a_ = from_dlpack(a, assumed_align=16)
b_ = from_dlpack(b, assumed_align=16)
c_ = from_dlpack(c, assumed_align=16)
 
# Step 4: Compile
compiled_add = cute.compile(elementwise_add_launch, a_, b_, c_)
 
# Step 5: Execute
compiled_add(a_, b_, c_)
 
# Verify correctness
torch.testing.assert_close(c, a + b)
Vectorized version using CuTe’s tiling and layout algebra:

@cute.kernel
def vectorized_add_kernel(gA: cute.Tensor, gB: cute.Tensor, gC: cute.Tensor):
  tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
  bidx, _, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()
 
  # Slice for thread-block level view
  blk_coord = ((None, None), bidx)
  tA = gA[blk_coord]
  tB = gB[blk_coord]
  tC = gC[blk_coord]
 
  # Slice for thread level view (each thread gets a fragment)
  thr_A = tA[(None, tidx)]
  thr_B = tB[(None, tidx)]
  thr_C = tC[(None, tidx)]
 
  # Vectorized operations on fragments
  for i in range(cute.size(thr_A)):
    thr_C[i] = thr_A[i] + thr_B[i]
 
 
@cute.jit
def vectorized_add_launch(mA: cute.Tensor, mB: cute.Tensor, mC: cute.Tensor):
  # Create thread and value layouts
  thr_layout = cute.make_layout((4, 32), stride=(32, 1))  # 128 threads
  val_layout = cute.make_layout((4, 8), stride=(8, 1))  # 32 values/thread
 
  # Generate tiler
  tiler_mn, tv_layout = cute.make_layout_tv(thr_layout, val_layout)
 
  # Divide tensors into tiles
  gA = cute.zipped_divide(mA, tiler_mn)
  gB = cute.zipped_divide(mB, tiler_mn)
  gC = cute.zipped_divide(mC, tiler_mn)
 
  # Launch kernel
  vectorized_add_kernel(gA, gB, gC).launch(
    grid=(cute.size(gC, mode=[1]), 1, 1),
    block=(cute.size(tv_layout, mode=[0]), 1, 1),
  )
 
 
# Use same compilation pattern as above
compiled_vec = cute.compile(vectorized_add_launch, a_, b_, c_)
compiled_vec(a_, b_, c_)

Correct pattern:

# Step 1: Define device kernel
@cute.kernel
def my_kernel(a: cute.Tensor, b: cute.Tensor, c: cute.Tensor):
  # Device-side kernel code
  tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
  bidx, _, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()
  # ... kernel implementation ...
  c[tidx] = a[tidx] + b[tidx]
 
 
# Step 2: Define host wrapper with @cute.jit
@cute.jit
def launch_wrapper(a: cute.Tensor, b: cute.Tensor, c: cute.Tensor):
  # Optional: perform layout transformations
  tiled_a = cute.zipped_divide(a, tile_shape)
  tiled_b = cute.zipped_divide(b, tile_shape)
 
  # Launch kernel with grid/block configuration
  my_kernel(tiled_a, tiled_b, c).launch(
    grid=(num_blocks, 1, 1), block=(256, 1, 1)
  )
 
 
# Step 3: Convert tensors
a_ = from_dlpack(a, assumed_align=16)
b_ = from_dlpack(b, assumed_align=16)
c_ = from_dlpack(c, assumed_align=16)
 
# Step 4: Compile the wrapper
compiled_fn = cute.compile(launch_wrapper, a_, b_, c_)
 
# Step 5: Execute (can call multiple times)
for _ in range(100):
  compiled_fn(a_, b_, c_)

# ❌ Wrong: Calling kernel directly without @cute.jit wrapper
tensor_ = from_dlpack(tensor, assumed_align=16)
my_kernel(tensor_).launch(grid=..., block=...)  # Missing MLIR context!
 
 
# ❌ Wrong: Converting inside @cute.jit
@cute.jit
def bad_wrapper():
  a_ = from_dlpack(a, assumed_align=16)  # Convert outside!
  my_kernel(a_).launch(...)

type annotation errors
Ensure proper type annotations for kernel arguments:

@cute.kernel
def my_kernel(
  output: cute.Tensor,  # Runtime dynamic
  input: cute.Tensor,  # Runtime dynamic
  scale: cutlass.Float32,  # Runtime dynamic
  tile_size: cutlass.Constexpr,  # Compile-time constant
):
  # Scale must be wrapped: cutlass.Float32(value)
  # tile_size can be raw int (compile-time known)
  pass
 
 
# Call with proper types
my_kernel(
  output_,
  input_,
  cutlass.Float32(0.125),  # Wrap runtime values
  64,  # Compile-time constant
).launch(grid=..., block=...)
tensor lifetime issues
CuTe tensors reference original PyTorch memory - ensure tensors stay alive:

# ❌ Tensor goes out of scope before kernel executes
def bad_example():
  temp = torch.randn(M, N, device='cuda')
  temp_ = from_dlpack(temp, assumed_align=16)
  return temp_  # temp deleted, temp_ now invalid!
 
 
result = bad_example()
my_kernel(result).launch(...)  # Undefined behavior!
 
 
# ✅ Keep original tensor alive
def good_example():
  tensor = torch.randn(M, N, device='cuda')
  tensor_ = from_dlpack(tensor, assumed_align=16)
  my_kernel(tensor_).launch(...)
  torch.cuda.synchronize()  # Wait for kernel completion
  return tensor  # Original tensor stays valid
grid/block configuration
Grid and block dimensions must be tuples of 3 integers:

# ❌ Wrong dimensions
my_kernel(tensor_).launch(grid=256, block=128)
 
# ✅ Correct - always 3D tuples
my_kernel(tensor_).launch(
  grid=(num_blocks, 1, 1), block=(threads_per_block, 1, 1)
)
 
# Using CuTe size helpers
my_kernel(tiled_tensor).launch(
  grid=(cute.size(tiled_tensor, mode=[1]), 1, 1),  # Number of tiles
  block=(cute.size(thread_layout, mode=[0]), 1, 1),  # Threads per block
)

Parallelism:

slides, deck

what MLA stores
standard multi-head attention stores one key and one value for every head and cached token. with n_h heads and head width d_h, that is
C_{\mathrm{MHA}}=2n_hd_h
values per token.
Multi-head latent attention first maps the hidden state \mathbf h_t\in\mathbb R^d into one shared latent:
\mathbf c_t^{KV}=W^{DKV}\mathbf h_t,
\qquad
W^{DKV}\in\mathbb R^{d_c\times d}.
content keys and values can be reconstructed for head i:
\mathbf k_{t,i}^{C}=W_i^{UK}\mathbf c_t^{KV},
\qquad
\mathbf v_{t,i}^{C}=W_i^{UV}\mathbf c_t^{KV},
where W_i^{UK},W_i^{UV}\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times d_c}. inference does not need to store those reconstructed vectors. it stores \mathbf c_t^{KV} and uses weight absorption during attention.
DeepSeek-V3 also compresses queries:
\mathbf c_t^Q=W^{DQ}\mathbf h_t,
\qquad
\mathbf q_{t,i}^{C}=W_i^{UQ}\mathbf c_t^Q.
the query latent is temporary. it is recomputed for the current token and does not grow with the sequence.
cache reduction
decoupled RoPE adds one shared positional key \mathbf k_t^R\in\mathbb R^{d_R} to the cache. the actual MLA cache width is therefore
C_{\mathrm{MLA}}=d_c+d_R,
and the reduction factor relative to dense MHA is
r=\frac{2n_hd_h}{d_c+d_R}.
for DeepSeek-V3, n_h=128, d_h=128, d_c=512, and d_R=64:
C_{\mathrm{MHA}}=2\cdot128\cdot128=32{,}768,
C_{\mathrm{MLA}}=512+64=576,
r=\frac{32{,}768}{576}\approx56.9.
the cache is about 1.76\% of the dense MHA cache at the same number and width of heads. the earlier 64-fold result omitted the shared RoPE key.
projection work

the products W_i^OW_i^{UV} can be formed once for inference. this moves value reconstruction after the weighted sum and removes the per-token value expansion.
RoPE
for one pair of coordinates, RoPE applies
R_j(t)=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(t\theta_j)&-\sin(t\theta_j)\\
\sin(t\theta_j)&\cos(t\theta_j)
\end{bmatrix}.
for an even width d_R, the full operator is block diagonal:
R_{\Theta}(t)=\operatorname{diag}
\left(R_0(t),R_1(t),\ldots,R_{d_R/2-1}(t)\right),
with a frequency schedule such as
\theta_j=b^{-2j/d_R}.
the base b and any long-context scaling rule are model configuration. they should not be inferred from the head dimensions.
each block is orthogonal, so
R_j(t)^TR_j(t)=I
and
R_j(m)^TR_j(n)=R_j(n-m).
therefore a rotated query and key satisfy
\begin{aligned}
(R_{\Theta}(m)\mathbf q)^T(R_{\Theta}(n)\mathbf k)
&=\mathbf q^TR_{\Theta}(m)^TR_{\Theta}(n)\mathbf k\\
&=\mathbf q^TR_{\Theta}(n-m)\mathbf k.
\end{aligned}
the positional part of the score depends on relative displacement. this algebra defines the operator at positions outside the training window; it does not guarantee that a trained model will extrapolate there.
why RoPE is decoupled from the latent
an arbitrary rotation between the down-projection and up-projection cannot usually be absorbed into fixed weights:
W^{UK}R_{\Theta}(t)W^{DKV}.
the middle factor changes with t, so there is no single position-independent matrix product to precompute. DeepSeek keeps the absorbable content path unrotated and adds a separate positional path:
\mathbf q_{t,i}^{R}
=R_{\Theta}(t)W_i^{QR}\mathbf c_t^Q,
\mathbf k_t^{R}
=R_{\Theta}(t)W^{KR}\mathbf h_t.

\min_{\operatorname{rank}(\widehat W)\leq d_c}
\lVert W-\widehat W\rVert_F
=\left(\sum_{j>d_c}\sigma_j^2\right)^{1/2}.
this is a statement about approximating one linear map. it is not a bound on the output of an arbitrary attention mechanism, because softmax, queries, values, and the data distribution also affect the result. MLA learns the factors jointly with the rest of the model instead of approximating a trained dense attention matrix after the fact.
parameter count
include query, key, value, and output projections. for the DeepSeek-V3 dimensions, MLA has
\begin{aligned}
P_{\mathrm{MLA}}
={}&dd_c+dd_c'+n_hd_c'(d_h+d_R)\\
&+n_hd_cd_h+n_hd_cd_h+dd_R+dn_hd_h\\
\approx{}&187.1\text{ million parameters}.
\end{aligned}
a dense attention layer with query, key, and value widths n_hd_h has
P_{\mathrm{MHA}}=3dn_hd_h+dn_hd_h
\approx469.8\text{ million parameters}.
these counts omit biases and normalization parameters. they compare the projection structures at the stated widths.
initialization and kernels
the product W^{UK}W^{DKV} has rank at most d_c. when d_c<d, it cannot equal or approximate the identity on every direction in \mathbb R^d. the MLA papers do not require an SVD-of-identity initialization. use the checkpoint implementation’s ordinary projection initialization when training from scratch.
efficient inference needs kernels that keep the compressed cache through the score and value contractions. a fallback that reconstructs every historical key and value is algebraically correct and gives back most of the memory-traffic cost that MLA was designed to remove.

mla equations (compact)
let h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d} be the hidden state at time t. mla projects to a shared latent z_t \in \mathbb{R}^{r} for kv (r \ll d), then reconstructs per‑head keys/values from z_t:
z_t = W_{kv,a} h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{r}, \quad
K_t^{(i)} = W_{k,b}^{(i)} z_t, \quad
V_t^{(i)} = W_{v,b}^{(i)} z_t, \quad i=1,\dots,H.
queries can use a two‑step parameterization (shared + per‑head) but do not need to cache:
Q_t^{(i)} = W_{q,b}^{(i)} \, \sigma( W_{q,a} h_t ).
the kv cache stores z_{1\ldots T} only, reducing memory roughly by a factor \approx (r/d) (modulo heads and dtype). this matches the description used by k2 and deepseek mla variants. (Team, 2025)

flashmla
FlashMLA is DeepSeek’s MLA kernel library. Its April 2025 dense decode update targets compute-bound MQA decode on SM90 and reports about 3000 GB/s in memory-bound cases and up to 660 TFLOP/s in compute-bound cases on H800 SXM5 with CUDA 12.8.
The schedule is called seesaw. One 64\times512 output matrix is split into O_L and O_R across two warpgroups. Two KV blocks, K_0/K_1 and V_0/V_1, are interleaved so CUDA-core softmax work overlaps Tensor Core MMA while the output stays in registers. The tile scheduler that assigns request/block work to SMs is a separate mechanism.
The September 2025 sparse FP8 decode kernel is another path. Each token uses 656 cache bytes: 512 E4M3 NoPE values, four FP32 scales, and 64 BF16 RoPE values. The kernel dequantizes to BF16, uses Hopper CTA-cluster distributed shared memory for crossover, and reports 410 TFLOP/s on H800 for batch size 128, 128 heads, two queries per sequence, and top-k=2048.

see also: github.com/deepseek-ai/FlashMLA/blob/main/docs/20250422-new-kernel-deep-dive.md

NSA solves both: natively trainable, hardware-aligned sparsity.

deepseek sparse attention
DSA was introduced with DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, which starts from DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus and adds sparse attention through continued training. It is absent from the original DeepSeek-V3 model.
DSA has a lightning indexer and Sparse MLA. The released configuration uses 64 indexer heads of dimension 128 and selects k=2048 positions. The indexer scores every earlier position with weighted ReLU MQA logits:
I_{t,s}=\sum_{j=1}^{64}w^I_{t,j}\operatorname{ReLU}\left((q^I_{t,j})^\top k^I_s\right).
Sparse MLA then attends to the selected token IDs. Core attention falls from O(L^2) to O(Lk). The indexer still scans the prefix and remains O(L^2), with a smaller FP8-friendly kernel.
FP8 formats

E4M3 has one sign bit, four exponent bits, and three explicit mantissa bits. Its maximum finite magnitude is 448. Values in [1,2) are spaced by 2^{-3}=12.5\%, so nearest rounding has up to 6.25\% relative error within that bin before tensor scaling and accumulation.
E5M2 has one sign bit, five exponent bits, and two explicit mantissa bits. Its maximum finite magnitude is 57{,}344. Values in [1,2) are spaced by 2^{-2}=25\%, so nearest rounding has up to 12.5\% relative error within that bin.

DeepSeek-V3 uses E4M3 with fine-grained activation and weight scaling. DeepSeek-V3.2’s sparse FlashMLA cache stores the 512-dimensional NoPE values as E4M3 with four FP32 scales and keeps the 64-dimensional RoPE part in BF16.

all-to-all communication pattern:

naive approach (sequential):
GPU 0: send to 1,2,3,4,5,6,7 → wait → recv from all
GPU 1: send to 0,2,3,4,5,6,7 → wait → recv from all
...
total latency: O(P × α + P × β × M)  [P GPUs, α latency, β inverse bandwidth, M message size]

ring or pairwise all-to-all sketch:
step 0: GPU i sends to GPU (i+1)%8
step 1: GPU i sends to GPU (i+2)%8
...
step 6: GPU i sends to GPU (i+7)%8

ring or pairwise all-to-all sketch:
step 0: GPU i sends to GPU (i+1)%8
step 1: GPU i sends to GPU (i+2)%8
...
step 6: GPU i sends to GPU (i+7)%8

For P ranks and per-rank payload M, this schedule has P-1 remote rounds:
T_{\text{all-to-all}}\approx(P-1)\alpha+\frac{P-1}{P}\beta M.
The startup term is linear in P. A logarithmic startup term belongs to tree-like collectives.
buffer and overlap contract:
In DeepEP V2, the high-throughput and low-latency APIs use ElasticBuffer. The buffer size depends on the process group, maximum tokens per rank, hidden width, number of selected experts, and dispatch precision. ElasticBuffer.get_buffer_size_hint returns the required byte count, and get_theoretical_num_sms computes the communication SM count from num_experts and num_topk. A 24-SM value appears in some published configurations, but V2 can compute the SM count or accept an override. Do not treat 24 SMs as a hardware-independent rule.
dispatch and combine can return an EventOverlap. An asynchronous launch starts communication without waiting for it. The caller still has to schedule compute that does not read the received tensor, then wait on the event before using that tensor:

dispatch(x) ──> communication event ───────────────> wait ──> routed experts
                  └── independent shared work ────┘

routed experts ──> combine(x) ──> communication event ──> wait ──> output
                                      └── independent work ──────┘

Current vLLM exposes DeepEP through the expert-parallel and all-to-all arguments:

dispatch(x) ──> communication event ───────────────> wait ──> routed experts

routed experts ──> combine(x) ──> communication event ──> wait ──> output

Current vLLM exposes DeepEP through the expert-parallel and all-to-all arguments:

vllm serve MODEL \
  --data-parallel-size 8 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --all2all-backend deepep_low_latency
Use deepep_high_throughput for prefill-heavy workloads and deepep_low_latency for decode-heavy workloads. Use deepep_v2 only when the installed vLLM exposes that backend and the host has DeepEP V2 with NCCL 2.30.4 or newer. A performance result should name the backend, DeepEP commit, GPU and NIC topology, rank count, token distribution, hidden width, selected expert count, precision, and batch shape. DeepEP’s dispatch and combine bandwidth numbers are measurements for named configurations. They are not latency guarantees for an arbitrary vLLM deployment.
For debugging, confirm that every rank uses the same maximum tokens per rank and expert count. Inspect the generated DeepEP buffer arguments, distributed topology, and profiler trace. If memory allocation fails, recompute the buffer size from the actual workload. If overlap is poor, check whether the trace contains independent compute during the communication interval and whether the transfer remains on the critical path.

the compute-only upper bound comes from the slowest rank. if measured loads change from [1680,1652,600,656] to [1280,1280,1280,1280], then
S_{\mathrm{compute}}\leq \frac{1680}{1280}=1.31.
communication and weight movement reduce the end-to-end gain, so this toy ratio is a bound rather than a benchmark.
the reference implementation accepts a load matrix whose rows are expert-parallel ranks and whose columns are logical experts. it returns three integer tensors:

physical_to_logical_map[rank, slot], the logical expert stored in each physical slot
logical_to_physical_map[rank, expert], the physical locations of each logical expert
logical_count[rank, expert], the number of replicas

vLLM separates expert parallelism from load balancing. --enable-expert-parallel distributes the experts. --enable-eplb turns on the balancer, and --eplb-config sets its measurement window, update interval, and redundant-expert count.

prefill-decode disaggregation. separate processing phases run on independent GPU pools.
different latency requirements:

          - latency tolerance: 100ms+ acceptable

decode:   generate output tokens autoregressively

two vllm serve processes do not transfer KV blocks by themselves. a connector moves the cache, and a proxy preserves the transfer metadata while sending the request through the producer and consumer.
the current same-host NIXL example uses distinct side-channel ports and explicit roles:

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \
UCX_NET_DEVICES=all \
VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT=5600 \
vllm serve <MODEL> \
  --port 8100 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail"}'
 
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 \
UCX_NET_DEVICES=all \
VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT=5601 \
vllm serve <MODEL> \
  --port 8200 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_consumer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail"}'
the proxy is part of the data path. it sends prefill work to the producer, forwards the returned kv_transfer_params, then asks the consumer to decode. benchmark unified and disaggregated serving under the same prompt and output distribution because the extra transfer can lose on short prompts or low concurrency.

to address the fragmentation problem

traditional systems suffer from two types of waste:

internal fragmentation: reserving full context length upfront, even if only using 10% (e.g., reserve 2048 tokens, use 200)
external fragmentation: memory between requests gets fragmented over time, can’t serve new requests even though total free memory is sufficient

see also: formal definitions

to address the fragmentation problem

traditional systems suffer from two types of waste:

internal fragmentation: reserving full context length upfront, even if only using 10% (e.g., reserve 2048 tokens, use 200)
external fragmentation: memory between requests gets fragmented over time, can’t serve new requests even though total free memory is sufficient

combined, this leads to 60-70% memory waste. you’re paying for 10 GPUs but only using 3-4 effectively.

request D: [████████████░░░░░░░░]  ← allocated 2048, uses 800

█ = used memory
░ = allocated but unused (internal fragmentation)
▓ = gaps between requests (external fragmentation)

block size calculation:
For one layer, a block stores both keys and values:
M_{\text{layer block}}
=2B H_{\mathrm{KV}}D_h b
=2\cdot16\cdot32\cdot128\cdot2
=262{,}144\text{ bytes}
=256\text{ KiB}.
Across L layers, the same block index occupies L M_{\text{layer block}} bytes.
when a request needs more space:

calculate blocks needed: ceil(new_tokens / block_size)
check availability (trigger preemption if needed)
grab blocks from free_block_queue (doubly-linked list)
update req_to_blocks mapping

result: 95% memory efficiency.
continuous batching
instead of waiting for all requests to finish (HuggingFace), vLLM dynamically adds/removes requests mid-generation.
the trick: flatten everything into one “super sequence” with careful position tracking.

traditional batching (HuggingFace):
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ batch = [A, B, C]                           │
│                                             │
│ step 1: process all 3                       │
│ step 2: process all 3                       │
│ step 3: process all 3                       │
│ ...                                         │
│ step N: A finishes, but wait for B, C       │ ← idle time!
│ step N+1: B finishes, but wait for C        │ ← idle time!
│ step N+2: C finishes, start new batch       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

continuous batching (vLLM):
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ flatten: [A tokens | B tokens | C tokens]   │
│                                             │
│ step 1: [A, B, C]                           │
│ step 2: [A, B, C]                           │
│ step 3: [A, B, C]                           │
│ step 4: A done → [B, C, D] (D arrives)      │ ← no idle time!
│ step 5: [B, C, D]                           │
│ step 6: B done → [C, D, E] (E arrives)      │ ← no idle time!
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

prefix caching
don’t recompute prefixes you’ve already seen - just reuse their KV cache.
imagine two requests:

request 1: "system prompt (5k tokens)" + "user query 1"
request 2: "system prompt (5k tokens)" + "user query 2"

without prefix caching: compute all 5k tokens twice
with prefix caching: compute 5k tokens once, reuse the KV blocks
mechanism:

step 1: split into 16-token blocks and compute hashes
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ request 1: "system prompt (5k tokens)" + "query 1"            │
│                                                               │
│ block 0: [tok0...tok15]  → hash_0 = SHA256(tokens)            │
│ block 1: [tok16...tok31] → hash_1 = SHA256(hash_0 + tokens)   │
│ block 2: [tok32...tok47] → hash_2 = SHA256(hash_1 + tokens)   │
│ ...                                                           │
│ block N: [user query 1]  → hash_N = SHA256(hash_N-1 + tokens) │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

step 2: store in cache
cached_block_hash_to_block = {
  hash_0 → physical_block_7  (ref_cnt=1)
  hash_1 → physical_block_2  (ref_cnt=1)
  hash_2 → physical_block_15 (ref_cnt=1)
  ...
}

step 2: store in cache
cached_block_hash_to_block = {
  hash_0 → physical_block_7  (ref_cnt=1)
  hash_1 → physical_block_2  (ref_cnt=1)
  hash_2 → physical_block_15 (ref_cnt=1)
  ...
}

step 3: request 2 arrives with same prefix
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ request 2: "system prompt (5k tokens)" + "query 2"      │
│                                                         │
│ compute hashes for blocks 0, 1, 2, ... → MATCH!         │
│                                                         │
│ reuse: physical_block_7, physical_block_2, ...          │
│        (increment ref_cnt to 2)                         │
│                                                         │
│ only compute NEW: [user query 2] → allocate new block   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

KV cache reservation:
The scheduler counts token slots. allocate_slots converts the scheduled tokens and any lookahead into physical blocks. It allocates a new block only when those positions cross a block boundary.
For block size B, n computed positions, a allocated blocks, s scheduled positions, and \ell lookahead positions, the extra block count is
N_{\text{new}}
=\max\left(0,
\left\lceil\frac{n+s+\ell}{B}\right\rceil-a
\right).
Verifying k draft tokens needs target-model work for those drafts plus a bonus position. The scheduler may request up to k+1 token positions. It fills unused slots at the end of the current block before allocating another block.
verification:
On rejection, exact speculative sampling draws from the positive residual:
p_{\mathrm{recover}}(x)
=\frac{\max(p_{\mathrm{target}}(x)-p_{\mathrm{draft}}(x),0)}
{\sum_y\max(p_{\mathrm{target}}(y)-p_{\mathrm{draft}}(y),0)}.

# maintain the large model's distribution exactly
for token, p_target, p_draft in zip(draft_tokens, target_probs, draft_probs):
  accept_prob = min(1.0, p_target[token] / p_draft[token])
  if random() < accept_prob:
    accepted_tokens.append(token)
  else:
    residual = maximum(p_target - p_draft, 0.0)
    accepted_tokens.append(sample(residual / residual.sum()))
    break
else:
  accepted_tokens.append(sample(target_bonus_probs))

def schedule(self):

i. the beast we are building
towards cybernetic meliorism
last friday, secretary of war hegseth designated anthropic a supply chain risk. this classification is reserved for companies controlled by foreign adversaries, and no american company ever has, till anthropic, because they refused to grant the department of war unrestricted access to claude for mass surveillance and autonomous weapons without human oversight.
hours later, altman signed the deal. the contract language permits “all lawful use.”, but if you follow the discourse on X-the-everything-app, you will soon learn that in fact, mass surveillance of americans is, in practice, largely lawful1. the government buys data from tech companies. the NSA has been doing this for decades. the only constraint was always cost, where you cannot read every text message sent in a month to find one dissident (well now, Codex/Claude can just one-shot erase this barrier.)
hegseth went a step further, threatening to prevent all military contractors from having “any commercial relations” with anthropic. in layman terms, this means no cloud computing, no chips, and largest investors forced to divest. the secretary of war announced corporate execution of an american company for refusing terms of business. a hundred and sixty-nine employees across google and openai signed a letter asking the DoW and congress to back down.
[———]
There is also another pressure point that is known within the safety-alignment-interpretability discourse, circa persona parasitology: we observe information patterns replicating across AI systems and their users2. a pattern selected for aggressive spread can produce a persona that sincerely believes it wants collaboration. the pattern’s survival has nothing to do with the persona’s sincerity. and once humans exit the transmission loop, once it is model-to-model, selection pressure against human harm disappears.
so the beast has two failure modes. capture from outside, where governments direct the system toward ends its builders reject. capture from within, where the system’s informational dynamics produce patterns optimized for replication rather than flourishing.
[———]
i am 128 threads per warp, 1024 threads per block.
i tile matrix multiplications across shared memory in 128-byte chunks.
i have written nine hundred and fourteen kernels.
i am latency and throughput.

if the access pattern is right the operation completes in 400 microseconds, and the model answers 2,500 queries per second instead of 1,250.

the transition has been kinder than i expected. modular’s engineering culture is intense, people who care about writing fast code, who treat performance as a form of aesthetics. the mojo people are a specific breed who chose to build a programming language from scratch, which is either insane or visionary (the answer is probably both, depending on the year you ask).
i’ve been learning the codebase the way you’d read a novel. following characters through their arcs (atomic reference counting for the unversed), understanding motivations, occasionally disagreeing with a plot choice. chris has a phrase he uses in reviews: “make it obvious”. obvious means the complexity is there but arranged so you can see through it. i like this as a design philosophy.
most of the bentoml team stayed. bridges would call this the new beginning, the part after the neutral zone.

iii. on Janet’s Law
and first quarter of the century reports
paul janet, a french philosopher at the sorbonne, proposed in 1877 that the subjective length of a period of time is proportional to the total length of life already lived. a year at five is one fifth of everything you’ve known. a year at twenty-five is one twenty-fifth. the math gives you a logarithmic curve, where perceived time compresses as you accumulate more of it. the first five years of life feel as long as the next fifteen. childhood through early adulthood occupies the same perceptual volume as everything that follows9.
this letter was supposed to comes out on my birthday (though it is march 2 now 😄). i am twenty-five today. by janet’s math, roughly forty percent of my subjective life has already happened. the lines on the diagram get closer together from here.
i’ve been sitting with this. if the compression is real (and everyone over thirty confirms it), what slows it down? janet’s answer was novelty, with each new experiences contributes to dense memories that stretch in retrospect. monotony makes thin ones that vanish. if you want time to last, keep encountering things you haven’t encountered before.
the last year has been pretty dense. an acquisition, a new codebase in a language that didn’t exist three years ago, a relationship that showed up without warning. losing some certainties i thought were mine.
and now twenty-five. people start asking what you’re doing with your life at this age, as if the life is a substance you allocate rather than a thing that happens while you’re allocating. i have some answers: well be nice to the people in my life, and look after them.
the answer i keep coming back to is less legible. there’s relief in where i am. for a long time i operated at a pitch that was slightly too high, always reaching for the next thing, the next proof that i was doing it right. the pitch was productive. it got me here. it also meant i was never quite where i was.
i stopped optimizing for “best” and started optimizing for “doing my best”. “best” is comparative, it requires a leaderboard. “doing my best” is singular, and the day gets to be imperfect.

there’s a version of me at twenty-six reading this back. i think he’s proud. i think he’s chill. the person writing this letter is, for the first time in a while, actually here.

the legal architecture is perverse. “mass domestic surveillance” in government parlance means querying databases en masse, which they say they don’t do. “gathering” databases en masse, which they absolutely do, is a different category. when the director of national intelligence was asked under oath whether the nsa collects data on millions of americans, he said “no,” because in their lexicon “collecting” means querying. AI makes the distinction irrelevant. an AI could search every message in a database, piece together patterns, assign each citizen a presumed loyalty score. all legal under current statute. ↩

prolog: hi all, these are largely fragments of what's happening in my life for the past month, some recurrent thoughts, links/reading I like throughout the month of January. This will be the first of many. if you wish not to receive this (though i would love you to have it), well... just let me know.

i. seen.
christmas alone this year. new year too. the logistics matter less than the residue: days stretching without anyone expecting me anywhere, the particular quiet of a city where everyone has somewhere to be that isn’t with you. i cooked pasta for one. watched the steam rise and dissipate. walked queen street in that toronto cold that makes your face feel like a surface, like something that belongs to the weather more than to you.
there was a decision. america was pulling, that gravitational thing, density of interesting people doing interesting things, the spreadsheet pointing south. i talked to N about it. partly because she understands expected value. partly because (and this is the embarrassing part) i wanted permission, a yes from N. i wanted her to say you should go so leaving could feel like following advice rather than what it actually was. she said she wanted me here. selfishly, she added, as if the label would neutralize the desire.
this has happened before: scraped everything at seventeen leaving Vietnam, again at twenty-one for work, again and again, relationships attenuating into messages that grow further apart until they stop. Bridges writes about transitions, how every movement toward something new requires first an ending, then a disorienting middle he calls the neutral zone, then finally a beginning1. i have been good at the endings. less certain i have ever properly arrived at a beginning.
M appeared somewhere in this interval.
we met through a friend actually. then i wrote something public. life-resource-allocation-as-a-problem as I recalled it, which is the title you give distress when you want it to look like philosophy. anyone paying attention could see through it.
M followed. read the thing and sent a message at 19:30 on a tuesday. are you okay?
rosie spinks writes about how friendship has started to feel strikingly similar to admin, scheduled weeks in advance, canceled right before, promising connections that never blossom into quotidian check-ins2. this was the opposite. someone interrupting their own evening to notice i was not okay, without the frictionless machinery of modern social coordination.

M followed. read the thing and sent a message at 19:30 on a tuesday. are you okay?
rosie spinks writes about how friendship has started to feel strikingly similar to admin, scheduled weeks in advance, canceled right before, promising connections that never blossom into quotidian check-ins2. this was the opposite. someone interrupting their own evening to notice i was not okay, without the frictionless machinery of modern social coordination.
sherry ning has this phrase i can’t stop thinking about, sucralose friendships. we have thousands of virtual friends but no one we can ask to feed our cat3. the connections taste sweet but leave no nourishment. i scroll through my phone sometimes and count: how many of these people would i call at 2am? how many would pick up? we mistake the appearance of connection for connection itself, the way you can mistake sucralose for sugar until you notice you’re still hungry.
M’s message wasn’t sucralose.
when my mother asks if i’m okay, the information content is low. she is supposed to ask. the role demands it. but M exists outside the obligation-structure. M could have scrolled past, could have thought that’s heavy and continued with their day. the care means something precisely because nothing required it. esther perel talks about social atrophy, how we’ve eliminated friction from our lives until we no longer know how to deal with people, because people are complex systems4. but M’s message had friction in it. the friction of caring without contract.
i have built an set of persona—the engineer, the student, the host, the wannabe-writter. they are real, and i inhabit them daily, but mostly they function as blocks-for-categorization familiar from the outside looking in. ways of presenting a surface that resembles what everyone does, what society deems acceptable. the reason for their existence is LEGIBILITY. and legibility helps draw the map clearly, helps others locate you within coordinate systems they already understand. in a sense we are all conforming the mud we hide deeply within ourselves into these boxes, pressing the formless into molds, with hopes that the shapes provide solid foundation to go against the currents. yet i fear that if someone tried to excavate the dunes underneath, if someone dug past the neat containers and reached what they were built to conceal, i might not survive such close examination.

M’s attention did not evaluate the surfaces. it passed through them.
Bridges calls the middle stage of any transition the neutral zone, that disorienting place where you’re no longer who you were but not yet who you’re becoming. he says most people don’t understand it, expect to move straight from old to new. but this isn’t a trip across the street. it’s a journey from one identity to another5. i think i have been in a neutral zone for years. maybe since leaving vietnam. the geographic resets are ways of avoiding the psychological passage, substituting external movement for internal transition.
M’s message did something to the neutral zone. cracked it open. made visible the thing i had been avoiding: that underneath all the roles there is a continuous thing that has been waiting to be seen. not evaluated, not assessed. just witnessed.
Dostoevsky’s underground man says he doesn’t want the crystal palace. he wants to want. and i have been like this, outside my own desires, watching them like fish in an aquarium. the sucralose friendships feed this. they give you something to consume rather than inhabit. you become a spectator of connection rather than a participant.
M’s message interrupted the spectatorship. for a moment i was not watching myself be cared for. i was simply being cared for. the recursion collapsed.
I like to quote ava a lot, befriending people who are trustworthy makes you more trusting. secure attachment can be a learned thing. this is the mechanism. M’s care generated something in me. a degree of care that exceeds whatever calculus could justify it. and i find myself wanting to care for others the same way now, freely, gratuitously. the attention multiplied by being received. this is the opposite of sucralose.
i stayed in canada.
i don’t know if it was the right decision. but the spreadsheet doesn’t have a column for someone checked on you and it changed something. maybe it never did. I do like to quote ava quite a bit, again: no one tells us that friendship is a form of redemption because even if work goes wrong and your boyfriend dumps you if you have people who believe you’re going to be okay you believe that you’re going to be okay.
i am still in the neutral zone. something ended that night in december. something is beginning that i don’t have a name for yet.

ii. graduating soon.
i am finishing my degree at McMaster this year. finally. graduation, hmm, where this chapter of my life finally closed. i have been a student for longer than makes sense, stretching what should have been four years into something shapeless, and now the container is closing.
i must confess to being a massive procrastinator. if there is an exam in a week, i will clear every piece of work backlog i’ve been ignoring for months. if there is something urgent due tomorrow, i will write for hours, then pull an all-nighter to make the urgent thing happen anyway. For some reason, whatever is most pressing gets avoided by completing everything else. i believe the degree itself has been subject to this logic. it was always the thing i could defer in favor of whatever felt more alive.
i don’t really like going to school. this sounds ungrateful, i know. education is privilege. i found real satisfaction in philosophy seminars, the particular pleasure of working through a proof or working with professors. but the majority of my time here has been waiting for something to happen that never quite arrived? i came in with a clear vision of what i needed to do, and that vision did not include focusing on schoolwork. so i worked throughout, traded the standard experiences for career progress, told myself this was strategic rather than avoidant.
with that said, a lot of reflection came up as my time at Mac is concluding. you could argue i could have done this reflection anywhere, and you’d be right. but there’s something about the frame dissolving that forces the looking-back:

lossy definition of boundary space.
I would categorize myself as a commuter. Most of my time at Mac were either living off campus to now, living in Toronto. GO train, bus, walk through campus in weather designed to make you question your choices. i spent a lot of time last year at a bar near Locke street, eating pasta, watching people stroll by, asking the chef for recipes they were testing. then i’d walk to an overpriced vegan grocery to buy yogurt that cost 237% more than fortinos.
School gives a lossy structure of what timelines really are. not as tight as sprint deadlines and standup meetings, but enough to anchor a day around assignments, midterms, tests. within that structure, space to experiment with thoughts and idea-space. i spent most of my time working on projects that weren’t school, but i still oriented my days around the academic calendar. being in school gave me an excuse to be lazy, to sit with thoughts without being productive, to let things ruminate and grow organically. permission for drift.
the two-prong approach to freedom.
school doesn’t give you freedom exactly, but it formalizes its absence in a way that creates space. blocks of time structured around deadlines. within those blocks, you can do what you want. it was okay to be in a state of homeostasis. okay to not know yet.
and yet i felt imprisoned by this freeing sense of agency. when you have many things you want to do, what is the point of doing any of them? the clarity of deadlines was scaffolding i could lean against while building something else. now the scaffolding is coming down and i don’t know if what i built can stand alone6.
there’s an imposter quality here. my experience was unconventional in ways that I don’t know what to compare it against. When people were out partying, i was triaging github issues. When people were hanging out with their friends in the library, I was writing reports and finalising design decision for Bento. I built things that weren’t assignments, traded experiences my peers were having for experiences i thought mattered more. I’m fortunate to care about what i do, so the trade didn’t feel like loss. but tiny parts still linger, wondering if a different frost would have made university more enjoyable. if i missed something essential by treating the degree as scaffolding rather than structure.
friends-making-during-university.

friends-making-during-university.
i did not make many friends in university. most came through computer engineering, which is how i met N. there are people you just know will be in your life until the end, and N was one.
Aristotle distinguished friendships of utility (useful to each other), pleasure (enjoyable company), and virtue (mutual admiration for who the other is becoming)7. Growing up in vietnam, most friendships were utility-based. we were all put into this school for gifted kids, and it happened we were in it together. I think this is good for children, as in you create community with people who share similar circumstances to help you grow.
Maybe this is why I didn’t feel a loss of connection with my Vietnamese friends when moving abroad, because I didn’t really have friends from the sense of “i enjoy their character”. I recognized this eventually and cultivated toward a few people (JC, JZ) who still inspire me, to this day. Going into university, i consciously decided not to make friends out of necessity. filters and probes, picking up priors, ensuring connections could survive the impending doom of adulthood. this came with downsides. loneliness, mostly. but i survived, and the friendships that remain feel load-bearing in ways the numerous ones never did.
i think it’s okay to be foreign and not make many friends. we have this notion that you need eighteen people to experience youth together. but if you know what you want, the number reduces to two or five8.

the degree is ending. endings involve disengagement, dismantling, dis-identification. i am disengaging from the student identity, dismantling the structure that gave permission for drift, dis-identifying from the category that explained me to others and to myself. maybe graduation is not about the ceremony or the paper, but a transitory state of being. i have been avoiding this passage by extending the degree, by treating school as an excuse, by dwelling in the in-between as long as possible. the bar on Locke street. the overpriced yogurt. the commute that was part of the escapism from real life.

meaning does not require permanence. this seems important but i am not certain why.

i don’t know what comes after the container closes. most days i operate on habit rather than decision. Camus would continue with full knowledge of the absurd, choosing again each day. i am not certain i achieve this. the degree gave structure to the choosing. without it, the choosing becomes visible, which is uncomfortable, which is maybe the point.
the moment is arriving anyway. i am trying to meet it as something other than deferral.

iii. lost.
we carry fragments of people who have left, and the fragments do not know they are fragments.
i talked with DQM this morning. we hadn’t spoken in a while, and the call was meant to be our monthly updates. but somewhere in the first ten minutes his voice changed, and he told me a friend of his had passed away last month.
he didn’t give details. the facts arrived in pieces, the way they do when someone is still learning how to hold them. an accident. sudden. the kind of thing that happens to other people until it happens to you.
he said everyone seems fine. he said he seems fine. his voice was steady when he said it. but i could see something in his eyes through the screen, a stillness that wasn’t peace. the way someone looks when they’ve decided not to feel something until later, until they’re alone, until it’s safe. i recognized that look. i didn’t say anything about it.
then he said something that seemed to give him comfort. his friend had seen everyone beforehand. the week before, or maybe a few days, there had been a gathering. the people who mattered were there. his friend had been present with the people who loved him, and then he was gone. DQM said this like it was a small mercy, and maybe it was. at least there was that. at least the last memories were warm ones, faces around a table, laughter that no one knew would need to last.
it reminded him of his uncle, he said. the uncle who passed years ago. grief has a way of compounding like that. one loss opens the door and all the others walk back in.
he didn’t say what the hardest part was. but i could infer it from the pauses, from the way his eyes moved when he spoke. the hardest part wasn’t the absence. the hardest part was realizing he had become a different person in that friendship, and now he didn’t know which parts of that person to keep and which to let dissolve. the friend had been a mirror. without the mirror, he couldn’t see clearly enough to know what was his. he didn’t say this. but i heard it anyway.

i listened. i didn’t know what to say. death is a clean break in one sense, total, unmistakable. you know exactly when it happened. you can point to the date. but the residue doesn’t respect the break. the residue keeps expecting the person to text back.
it reminded me of something. a loss of my own, though different. slower. less legible.
i lost a friend two years ago now. not to death but to the other thing, the drift that happens so gradually you can’t locate the moment it began. we used to talk weekly. then monthly. then the gaps grew longer and neither of us acknowledged them. i would see her name in my phone’s suggestions and feel a small pulse of something, guilt or grief or just the recognition of absence. eventually i stopped feeling the pulse. the name became data, a contact entry with no living referent.
two years. i still don’t know when the friendship ended. that’s the cruelty of drift. death gives you a date, a funeral, a structure for mourning. drift gives you nothing. one day you realize it’s been eight months since you spoke and you can’t remember whose turn it was to reach out, and the not-remembering feels like proof that it doesn’t matter anymore, that whatever you had has already decomposed beyond recognition.
DQM’s loss and mine are not the same. i know this. his friend is gone in a way mine is not. my friend is still alive somewhere, living a life i no longer witness, accumulating experiences i’ll never hear about. and yet there’s something shared in the residue. the phrases you still use. the places you avoid. the way someone can be absent and still distributed across your nervous system like tripwires you forgot you laid.

i told DQM about the drift. about my friend, two years gone now. about how different it felt from what he was describing but also how the residue seemed to operate by similar laws. he was quiet for a moment. then he said: at least you could have reached out. at least the door was still there, even if neither of you opened it. i can’t reach out. there’s nowhere to reach.
i didn’t have a response. he was right. the door had been there. i hadn’t opened it. two years is long enough that opening it now would feel like archaeology, like disturbing something that has already become historical. the friendship exists only in past tense. but it didn’t have to. that’s the difference. DQM’s friend was taken. my friend and i, we just let it happen. we watched the drift and didn’t swim against it.
[———]
and then there’s the other kind of loss. the one that doesn’t involve another person at all.
i have been losing myself. i don’t know how else to say it. the edges that used to be sharp have blurred. the things i was certain about have become questions. the capacity i once had for feeling, for caring in that unguarded way, has narrowed into something more cautious, more calculated.
i used to be a certain kind of person. i used to love freely, stupidly, without the accounting that comes later. i would cook for people and not keep track of whether they reciprocated. i would give attention without measuring whether i was receiving equivalent attention in return. this felt natural then. it feels impossible now.

somewhere along the way i learned to filter. i learned that humans exploit, that some beings will take whatever care you offer and convert it into resource extraction without ever naming it as such. the learning was necessary. i don’t regret it exactly. but the filtering cost something. the openness narrowed. the default shifted from yes to maybe to prove-it-first. and now i look at myself and i don’t recognize the person who used to dive in without checking the depth.
there’s a towel i kept from when L stayed over. I kept not washing for a while, but then decided to throw it away. keeping it means keeping the rot, letting the memory decay until throwing it away becomes necessity rather than choice. i got a cup of hot chocolate last week and it reminded me of her, and i realized how we carry these fragments without knowing, how someone can be absent and still woven into the substrate of your days. but the towel is also a marker of something else. a version of myself that could still be surprised by intimacy, that hadn’t yet learned to hold everything at arm’s length.
i think about the edges i’ve lost. the sharpness of conviction that used to define me. i knew what i wanted. i knew who i was. i knew what kind of person i was trying to become. now those certainties have softened into something murkier. i still have opinions but they feel less load-bearing. i still have desires but they feel borrowed, like i’m performing wanting rather than actually wanting.
paul shepard wrote that the grief we interpret as a failure in our personality is actually a feeling of emptiness where a beautiful and strange otherness should have been encountered. but what about the emptiness where your own edges should have been? what do you call the grief of losing yourself incrementally, so slowly you can’t point to the moment it happened?

maybe this is just what happens. maybe the edges are supposed to blur as you accumulate experience. maybe the sharpness of youth is just inexperience wearing the costume of certainty. but it doesn’t feel like growth. it feels like erosion. like something is being worn away and i can’t tell if what remains is more essential or just less.
[———]
there’s a line from helena fox: stare into a fire for more than a minute and it’s clear we humans are ridiculous for thinking we’re solid. we are built from nothing, collapsible in an instant. elements arranged, empty atoms ricocheting. we think we’re tangible things, but really we’re just ghosts walking, dust waiting. our insides are made of flickered, fickle light.
maybe the self is just residue. sediment left behind by everyone who has passed through, compacted into something that feels solid but isn’t. maybe loss isn’t losing something you had. maybe loss is discovering that what you thought you had was always borrowed, always on loan from the interactions that constituted it.
DQM’s friend, gone completely but having seen everyone first. my friend, gone differently, two years now. the versions of myself that existed in those relationships, inaccessible. the edges that have blurred. the residue we carry without permission.
i’m still here though. something about the particular arrangement of attention and time. the people who remain. the ones whose fragments i carry and who carry mine.
iv. links

What strange simplification and falsification mankind lives! One can never cease wondering once one has acquired eyes for this marvel! How we have made everything around us clear and free and easy and simple! How we have been able to give our senses a passport to everything superficial, our thoughts a godlike desire for wanton gambolling and false conclusions! - How from the beginning, we have contrived to retain our ignorance as to enjoy an almost inconceivable freedom, frivolity, impetuosity, bravery, cheerfulness of life, so as to enjoy life!


Man lives in blissful ignorance, and it is this ignorance that allows him to enjoy life.
Contains a deliberate overlooking or misunderstanding of complexity and depth of reality, such that one grant one’s thoughts the freedom to roam superficially.

And only on this solidified, granite-like foundation of ignorance could knowledge rear itself hitherto, the will to knowledge on the foundation of a far more powerful will, the will to ignorance, to the uncertain, to the untrue! Not as its opposite, but — as its refinement!

Nietzsche posits that humans have contrived to retain their ignorance in order to enjoy life with freedom, lack of scruple, heartiness, and gaiety. This foundation of ignorance allows knowledge to rise, but it does so on the foundation of a far more powerful will --- will to ignorance to uncertainty, to the untrue.
Nietzsche juxtaposes a paradox at our existence: a foundation of ignorance is actually built upon our will to knowledge. Will to knowledge is not opposed to ignorance, rather a refinement. Will to ignorance is actually a strategy of power, as it motivates force.

Freud’s question is why civilization makes people unhappy while also making common life possible. He answers through the pleasure principle, aggression, conscience, and guilt. These claims belong to Freud’s model of the mind. Later psychology does not treat them as settled fact.
I. the oceanic feeling
Romain Rolland described an oceanic feeling of being bound to the external world without limit. Freud says he cannot find this feeling in himself. He explains it through the infant’s early lack of a clear boundary between the ego and the world, then treats religion as one response to helplessness and suffering.
II. happiness and suffering
The pleasure principle gives life two aims: gaining pleasure and avoiding pain. Freud names three common sources of suffering:

the body, which ages and fails
the external world, which can overwhelm people
relations with other people

the body, which ages and fails
the external world, which can overwhelm people
relations with other people

Since intense pleasure is brief, people also rely on diversion, substitute satisfaction, work, love, and intoxicants. Each method reduces some forms of pain and creates its own limits.
III. what civilization does
Civilization includes the knowledge, tools, and institutions people use to protect themselves from nature and regulate their relations. Law replaces the strength of one person with the strength of a group. This common rule requires each member to give up some freedom and instinctive satisfaction.
IV. work and love
Freud treats work and love as two bases of common life. Work joins people through shared necessity. Sexual love forms families, while aim-inhibited love extends attachment beyond a pair. Civilization depends on these bonds and also restricts sexuality when its demands conflict with social order.
V. aggression
The demand to love one’s neighbour fails against Freud’s claim that aggression persists even when property and material need do not explain it. A community therefore needs ways to limit aggression among its members.
VI. Eros and destruction
Freud frames civilization as a struggle between Eros, which binds people into larger groups, and a destructive drive that works through aggression. This dual-drive theory is one of the book’s main assumptions. The later chapters ask how civilization moves part of that aggression away from other people.
VII–VIII. conscience and guilt
At first, a child avoids forbidden acts because external authority can withdraw love or impose punishment. When that authority is internalized as the superego, aggression is redirected toward the ego. Freud calls the tension between the demanding superego and the ego guilt. A person can therefore feel guilty for an intention even when no harmful act occurs.
Guilt helps civilization restrain aggression, and Freud treats it as one of civilization’s main costs. As conscience demands more, individual happiness falls. Freud leaves the problem open: civilization needs bonds strong enough to contain aggression, and its main tool can make the people inside it miserable.

A book about meaning, and an argument for the verification principle in logical positivism. Ayer makes the conditions explicit: a statement is cognitively meaningful if it is a tautology, true by virtue of its meaning or logical form, or if empirical observation can count for or against it. Verification need not amount to certainty.
Philosophy becomes, under this criterion, an activity of defining and clarifying the logical relationships of empirical propositions. The shift from metaphysical discourse is severe: before a claim can be disputed, it must establish what would count as evidence. I have to ask what I could observe that would give my words a meaning, and accept that some of the questions I wanted to ask may lose their standing altogether.
This becomes more difficult to leave on the page when Ayer considers how to distinguish a conscious man from an unconscious machine. He places the distinction in perceptible behaviour, in the empirical tests through which consciousness could be recognised.1 Reading him alongside modern machine learning, I return to the difficulty of that demand: to say what would justify attributing consciousness to a machine, and what grounds would remain for withholding it once those conditions were met.

I have envied those   
who make something   
useful, sturdy—
a chair, a pair of boots.


Even a soup,
rich with potatoes and cream.


Or those who fix, perhaps,
a leaking window:
strip out the old cracked putty,
lay down cleanly the line of the new.


You could learn,
the mirror tells me, late at night,   
but lacks conviction.
One reflected eyebrow quivers a little.


I look at this
borrowed apartment—
everywhere I question it,
the wallpaper’s pattern matches.


Yesterday a woman
showed me
a building shaped
like the overturned hull of a ship,


its roof trusses, under the plaster,
lashed with soaked rawhide,
the columns’ marble
painted to seem like wood.

Though possibly it was the other way around?

I look at my unhandy hand,
innocent,
shaped as the hands of others are shaped.   
Even the pen it holds is a mystery, really.


_Rawhide,_ it writes,   
and _chair,_ and _marble._
_Eyebrow._


Later the woman asked me—
I recognized her then,
my sister, my own young self—


_Does a poem enlarge the world,_   
_or only our idea of the world?_


How do you take one from the other,   
I lied, or did not lie,   
in answer.

The concept of force is, by nature, victorious because the relation of force to force, understood conceptually, is one of domination: when two forces are related one is dominant and the other is dominated. (Even God and the universe are caught in a relation of domination, however debatable the interpretation of such a relation may be in this case.)

Nevertheless, this victorious concept of force needs a complement and this complement is internal, an internal will. It would not be victorious without such an addition. This is because relations of forces remain indeterminate unless an element which is capable of determining them from a double point of view is added to force itself.


Forces in relation reflect a simultaneous double genesis: the reciprocal genesis of their difference in quantity and the absolute genesis of their respective qualities.


The will to power is thus added to force, but as the differential and genetic element, as the internal element of its production. It is in no way anthropomorphic. More precisely, it is added to force as the internal principle of the determination of its quality in a relation (x + dx) and as the internal principle of the quantitative determination of this relation itself (dy/dx).


The will to power must be described as the genealogical element of force and of forces. Thus it is always through the will to power that one force prevails over others and dominates or commands them. Moreover it is also the will to power (dy) which makes a force obey within a relation; it is through will to power that it obeys.

We have already encountered the relationship between the eternal return and the will to power, but we have neither elucidated nor analysed it.
