“‘That woman Estelle,’” the note reads, “‘is partly the reason why George Sharp and I are separated today.’ Dirty crepe-de-Chine wrapper, hotel bar, Wilmington RR, 9:45 a.m. August Monday morning.”

Since the note is in my notebook, it presumably has some meaning to me. I study it for a long while. At first I have only the most general notion of what I was doing on an August Monday morning in the bar of the hotel across from the Pennsylvania Railroad station in Wilmington, Delaware (waiting for a train? missing one? 1960? 1961? why Wilmington?), but I do remember being there. The woman in the dirty crepe-de-Chine wrapper had come down from her room for a beer, and the bartender had heard before the reason why George Sharp and she were separated today. “Sure,” he said, and went on mopping the floor. “You told me.” At the other end of the bar is a girl. She is talking, pointedly, not to the man beside her but to a cat lying in the triangle of sunlight cast through the open door. She is wearing a plaid silk dress from Peck & Peck, and the hem is coming down.
Here is what it is: The girl has been on the Eastern Shore, and now she is going back to the city, leaving the man beside her, and all she can see ahead are the viscous summer sidewalks and the 3 a.m. long-distance calls that will make her lie awake and then sleep drugged through all the steaming mornings left in August (1960? 1961?). Because she must go directly from the train to lunch in New York, she wishes that she had a safety pin for the hem of the plaid silk dress, and she also wishes that she could forget about the hem and the lunch and stay in the cool bar that smells of disinfectant and malt and make friends with the woman in the crepe-de-Chine wrapper. She is afflicted by a little self-pity, and she wants to compare Estelles. That is what that was all about.

Why did I write it down? In order to remember, of course, but exactly what was it I wanted to remember? How much of it actually happened? Did any of it? Why do I keep a notebook at all? It is easy to deceive oneself on all those scores. The impulse to write things down is a peculiarly compulsive one, inexplicable to those who do not share it, useful only accidentally, only secondarily, in the way that any compulsion tries to justify itself. I suppose that it begins or does not begin in the cradle. Although I have felt compelled to write things down since I was five years old, I doubt that my daughter ever will, for she is a singularly blessed and accepting child, delighted with life exactly as life presents itself to her, unafraid to go to sleep and unafraid to wake up. Keepers of private notebooks are a different breed altogether, lonely and resistant rearrangers of things, anxious malcontents, children afflicted apparently at birth with some presentiment of loss.
My first notebook was a Big Five tablet, given to me by my mother with the sensible suggestion that I stop whining and learn to amuse myself by writing down my thoughts. She returned the tablet to me a few years ago; the first entry is an account of a woman who believed herself to be freezing to death in the Arctic night, only to find, when day broke, that she had stumbled onto the Sahara Desert, where she would die of the heat before lunch. I have no idea what turn of a five-year-old’s mind could have prompted so insistently “ironic” and exotic a story, but it does reveal a certain predilection for the extreme which has dogged me into adult life; perhaps if I were analytically inclined I would find it a truer story than any I might have told about Donald Johnson’s birthday party or the day my cousin Brenda put Kitty Litter in the aquarium.

So the point of my keeping a notebook has never been, nor is it now, to have an accurate factual record of what I have been doing or thinking. That would be a different impulse entirely, an instinct for reality which I sometimes envy but do not possess. At no point have I ever been able successfully to keep a diary; my approach to daily life ranges from the grossly negligent to the merely absent, and on those few occasions when I have tried dutifully to record a day’s events, boredom has so overcome me that the results are mysterious at best. What is this business about “shopping, typing piece, dinner with E, depressed”? Shopping for what? Typing what piece? Who is E? Was this “E” depressed, or was I depressed? Who cares?
In fact I have abandoned altogether that kind of pointless entry; instead I tell what some would call lies. “That’s simply not true,” the members of my family frequently tell me when they come up against my memory of a shared event. “The party was not for you, the spider was not a black widow, it wasn’t that way at all.” Very likely they are right, for not only have I always had trouble distinguishing between what happened and what merely might have happened, but I remain unconvinced that the distinction, for my purposes, matters. The cracked crab that I recall having for lunch the day my father came home from Detroit in 1945 must certainly be embroidery, worked into the day’s pattern to lend verisimilitude; I was ten years old and would not now remember the cracked crab. The day’s events did not turn on cracked crab. And yet it is precisely that fictitious crab that makes me see the afternoon all over again, a home movie run all too often, the father bearing gifts, the child weeping, an exercise in family love and guilt. Or that is what it was to me. Similarly, perhaps it never did snow that August in Vermont; perhaps there never were flurries in the night wind, and maybe no one else felt the ground hardening and summer already dead even as we pretended to bask in it, but that was how it felt to me, and it might as well have snowed, could have snowed, did snow.
How it felt to me: that is getting closer to the truth about a notebook.

I sometimes delude myself about why I keep a notebook, imagine that some thrifty virtue derives from preserving everything observed. See enough and write it down, I tell myself, and then some morning when the world seems drained of wonder, some day when I am only going through the motions of doing what I am supposed to do, which is write—on that bankrupt morning I will simply open my notebook and there it will all be, a forgotten account with accumulated interest, paid passage back to the world out there: dialogue overheard in hotels and elevators and at the hat-check counter in Pavillon (one middle-aged man shows his hat check to another and says, “That’s my old football number”); impressions of Bettina Aptheker and Benjamin Sonnenberg and Teddy (“Mr. Acapulco”) Stauffer; careful aperçus1 about tennis bums and failed fashion models and Greek shipping heiresses, one of whom taught me a significant lesson (a lesson I could have learned from F. Scott Fitzgerald, but perhaps we all must meet the very rich for ourselves) by asking, when I arrived to interview her in her orchid-filled sitting room on the second day of a paralyzing New York blizzard, whether it was snowing outside.
I imagine, in other words, that the notebook is about other people. But of course it is not. I have no real business with what one stranger said to another at the hat-check counter in Pavillon; in fact I suspect that the line “That’s my old football number” touched not my own imagination at all, but merely some memory of something once read, probably “The Eighty-Yard Run.”2 Nor is my concern with a woman in a dirty crepe-de-Chine wrapper in a Wilmington bar. My stake is always, of course, in the unmentioned girl in the plaid silk dress. Remember what it was to be me: that is always the point.

It is a difficult point to admit. We are brought up in the ethic that others, any others, all others, are by definition more interesting than ourselves; taught to be diffident, just this side of self-effacing. (“You’re the least important person in the room and don’t forget it,” Jessica Mitford’s3 governess would hiss in her ear on the advent of any social occasion; I copied that into my notebook because it is only recently that I have been able to enter a room without hearing some such phrase in my inner ear.) Only the very young and the very old may recount their dreams at breakfast, dwell upon self, interrupt with memories of beach picnics and favorite Liberty lawn dresses and the rainbow trout in a creek near Colorado Springs. The rest of us are expected, rightly, to affect absorption in other people’s favorite dresses, other people’s trout.
And so we do. But our notebooks give us away, for however dutifully we record what we see around us, the common denominator of all we see is always, transparently, shamelessly, the implacable “I.”

We are not talking here about the kind of notebook that is patently for public consumption, a structural conceit for binding together a series of graceful pensées4; we are talking about something private, about bits of the mind’s string too short to use, an indiscriminate and erratic assemblage with meaning only for its maker.
And sometimes even the maker has difficulty with the meaning. There does not seem to be, for example, any point in my knowing for the rest of my life that, during 1964, 720 tons of soot fell on every square mile of New York City, yet there it is in my notebook, labeled “FACT.” Nor do I really need to remember that Ambrose Bierce liked to spell Leland Stanford’s5 name “£eland $tanford” or that “smart women almost always wear black in Cuba,” a fashion hint without much potential for practical application. And does not the relevance of these notes seem marginal at best?:

Well, perhaps not entirely marginal. As a matter of fact, Mrs. Minnie S. Brooks and her MANDARIN COAT pull me back into my own childhood, for although I never knew Mrs. Brooks and did not visit Inyo County until I was thirty, I grew up in just such a world, in houses cluttered with Indian relics and bits of gold ore and ambergris and the souvenirs my Aunt Mercy Farnsworth brought back from the Orient. It is a long way from that world to Mrs. Lou Fox’s world, where we all live now, and is it not just as well to remember that? Might not Mrs. Minnie S. Brooks help me to remember what I am? Might not Mrs. Lou Fox help me to remember what I am not?
But sometimes the point is harder to discern. What exactly did I have in mind when I noted down that it cost the father of someone I know $650 a month to light the place on the Hudson in which he lived before the Crash? What use was I planning to make of this line by Jimmy Hoffa6: “I may have my faults, but being wrong ain’t one of them”? And although I think it interesting to know where the girls who travel with the Syndicate have their hair done when they find themselves on the West Coast, will I ever make suitable use of it? Might I not be better off just passing it on to John O’Hara7? What is a recipe for sauerkraut doing in my notebook? What kind of magpie keeps this notebook? “He was born the night the Titanic went down.” That seems a nice enough line, and I even recall who said it, but is it not really a better line in life than it could ever be in fiction?

But of course that is exactly it: not that I should ever use the line, but that I should remember the woman who said it and the afternoon I heard it. We were on her terrace by the sea, and we were finishing the wine left from lunch, trying to get what sun there was, a California winter sun. The woman whose husband was born the night the Titanic went down wanted to rent her house, wanted to go back to her children in Paris. I remember wishing that I could afford the house, which cost $1,000 a month. “Someday you will,” she said lazily. “Someday it all comes.” There in the sun on her terrace it seemed easy to believe in someday, but later I had a low-grade afternoon hangover and ran over a black snake on the way to the supermarket and was flooded with inexplicable fear when I heard the checkout clerk explaining to the man ahead of me why she was finally divorcing her husband. “He left me no choice,” she said over and over as she punched the register. “He has a little seven-month-old baby by her, he left me no choice.” I would like to believe that my dread then was for the human condition, but of course it was for me, because I wanted a baby and did not then have one and because I wanted to own the house that cost $1,000 a month to rent and because I had a hangover.
It all comes back.
Perhaps it is difficult to see the value in having one’s self back in that kind of mood, but I do see it; I think we are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be whether we find them attractive company or not. Otherwise they turn up unannounced and surprise us, come hammering on the mind’s door at 4 a.m. of a bad night and demand to know who deserted them, who betrayed them, who is going to make amends. We forget all too soon the things we thought we could never forget. We forget the loves and the betrayals alike, forget what we whispered and what we screamed, forget who we were.

I have already lost touch with a couple of people I used to be; one of them, a seventeen-year-old, presents little threat, although it would be of some interest to me to know again what it feels like to sit on a river levee drinking vodka-and-orange-juice and listening to Les Paul and Mary Ford8 and their echoes sing “How High the Moon” on the car radio. (You see I still have the scenes, but I no longer perceive myself among those present, no longer could even improvise the dialogue.) The other one, a twenty-three-year-old, bothers me more. She was always a good deal of trouble, and I suspect she will reappear when I least want to see her, skirts too long, shy to the point of aggravation, always the injured party, full of recriminations and little hurts and stories I do not want to hear again, at once saddening me and angering me with her vulnerability and ignorance, an apparition all the more insistent for being so long banished.

It is a good idea, then, to keep in touch, and I suppose that keeping in touch is what notebooks are all about. And we are all on our own when it comes to keeping those lines open to ourselves: your notebook will never help me, nor mine you. “So what’s new in the whiskey business?” What could that possibly mean to you? To me it means a blonde in a Pucci bathing suit sitting with a couple of fat men by the pool at the Beverly Hills Hotel. Another man approaches, and they all regard one another in silence for a while. “So what’s new in the whiskey business?” one of the fat men finally says by way of welcome, and the blonde stands up, arches one foot and dips it in the pool, looking all the while at the cabaña where Baby Pignatari is talking on the telephone. That is all there is to that, except that several years later I saw the blonde coming out of Saks Fifth Avenue in New York with her California complexion and a voluminous mink coat. In the harsh wind that day she looked old and irrevocably tired to me, and even the skins in the mink coat were not worked the way they were doing them that year, not the way she would have wanted them done, and there is the point of the story. For a while after that I did not like to look in the mirror, and my eyes would skim the newspapers and pick out only the deaths, the cancer victims, the premature coronaries, the suicides, and I stopped riding the Lexington Avenue IRT because I noticed for the first time that all the strangers I had seen for years—the man with the seeing-eye dog, the spinster who read the classified pages every day, the fat girl who always got off with me at Grand Central—looked older than they once had.
It all comes back. Even that recipe for sauerkraut: even that brings it back. I was on Fire Island when I first made that sauerkraut, and it was raining, and we drank a lot of bourbon and ate the sauerkraut and went to bed at ten, and I listened to the rain and the Atlantic and felt safe. I made the sauerkraut again last night and it did not make me feel any safer, but that is, as they say, another story.

Wittgenstein begins with Augustine’s picture of language as a system in which words name objects and sentences combine those names. The builders in §2 show that this picture works for one simple activity. The rest of the book asks what it leaves out.
language-games and use
In §7, Wittgenstein calls language joined with the activity around it a language-game. The examples in §23 include giving orders, reporting events, making jokes, thanking, cursing, and praying. Their differences matter because a word does its job within a practice.
Section 43 gives the line people usually quote: for a large class of cases, the meaning of a word is its use in the language. The qualification matters. Wittgenstein is giving a method for examining meaning, rather than a definition that covers every word.
family resemblance
Sections 65–67 ask what all games have in common. Wittgenstein finds overlapping similarities instead of one feature shared by every case. He calls this family resemblance. The point is practical: a concept can work without a boundary fixed by necessary and sufficient conditions.
This changes the philosophical question. Instead of assuming that a word hides one essence, inspect the cases in which people use it and the distinctions they already make.
following a rule
The rule-following discussion in §§185–202 examines what makes one application of a rule correct. An interpretation cannot settle the matter by itself because that interpretation can also be read in different ways. Section 202 locates the distinction between following a rule and merely thinking one is following it in a practice.
Training, correction, and repeated use give a rule its place in life. This does not require every competent speaker to recite an explicit theory of the rule. Competence appears in what the speaker goes on to do.
sensation and private signs
Sections 243–271 test the idea of a language whose words refer to sensations that only one speaker could identify. The diary example in §258 asks how a private sign could retain a standard of correct use if each application were checked only against whatever seemed right at the time.
These passages do not deny pain or inner life. They examine the grammar of sensation words and the public practices in which people learn and use them. The section has produced several competing arguments in the secondary literature, so it is safer to follow the examples than to compress them into one formal proof.

philosophy as clarification
Wittgenstein describes philosophy as work on confusions created by language. Section 109 calls it a struggle against the bewitchment of intelligence by language. Section 116 says that philosophy brings words back from metaphysical use to everyday use. Section 126 says philosophy puts familiar facts before us and describes them.
The aim is clarity about a particular problem. The book offers reminders, examples, and comparisons that let a misleading picture lose its grip. Its method begins with actual usage and stops when the source of the confusion is visible.

Freud begins by revising the earlier division between conscious, preconscious, and unconscious mental processes. Repressed material is unconscious, yet the unconscious also includes processes that were never repressed. Consciousness alone therefore cannot describe the organization of the mind.
the ego and the id
The ego is the organized part of mental life connected to perception and action. It develops from the id through contact with the external world. The id contains drives and wishes that do not follow the ego’s ordinary tests of consistency or external reality.
Freud describes the ego as trying to impose the reality principle on the id’s pursuit of pleasure. The ego controls action when it can, delays satisfaction, and tries to join the demands of the id to the conditions of the world. Its control is limited because much of the ego is also unconscious.
identification
An object-cathexis directs libidinal energy toward another person. When that relation is lost or abandoned, the ego can take the object into itself through identification. Freud uses melancholia as an early example: identification with the lost object changes the ego and allows the relation to persist internally.
He then gives identification a wider role in character. The ego contains traces of past object choices. This is one reason the structural model does not treat a person as a transparent, unified agent.
the superego
The superego, also called the ego ideal in parts of the text, develops from early identifications and the dissolution of the Oedipus complex. It preserves parental authority within the mind. It judges the ego, supplies ideals, and becomes a source of conscience and guilt.
This internal authority can be severe. Aggression that might have been directed outward can be taken up by the superego and turned against the ego. Freud later develops that account of guilt in Civilisation and its Discontents.
a divided ego
The ego faces pressure from the external world, the id, and the superego. These demands can conflict. A wish may seek immediate satisfaction, reality may block it, and the superego may condemn it before any action occurs. Freud uses this structure to explain why conscious intention gives an incomplete account of conduct.
The book is a theoretical model, not brain anatomy. It gives Freud distinctions for describing conflict inside a person. Those distinctions depend on assumptions about drives, development, and the Oedipus complex, which later psychology does not treat as settled fact.

Zarathustra attacks inherited categories of good and evil and asks how new values can be created. The overman names a direction of self-overcoming rather than a rule for conventional moral conduct. The eternal recurrence tests whether one could affirm a life in every detail.

The Tractatus is built from seven numbered propositions and decimal comments on them. Its argument moves from the structure of the world to the structure of propositions, then to the limits of what propositions can say.
facts and objects
Proposition 1 says that the world is everything that is the case. Proposition 1.1 restates this as a totality of facts rather than a collection of things. A fact is the existence of a state of affairs. A state of affairs is a possible combination of objects (§2.01).
Objects supply the stable possibilities within this system. Which combinations actually obtain determines the world. Wittgenstein calls the space of possible combinations logical space.
pictures and propositions
A picture represents a possible situation by arranging its elements in a structure. Its elements stand for objects, while their arrangement presents one way those objects could be related. The picture and the situation must share logical form for representation to occur (§2.18).
A proposition is a logical picture of a fact (§4.01). Its names correspond to objects, and its syntax presents a possible arrangement. The proposition has sense before anyone checks whether it is true. Reality then agrees or disagrees with the situation it depicts.
This account is compositional. The sense of a proposition depends on how its parts are arranged. It also explains why a proposition divides possibilities: it is true in the cases where the depicted situation obtains and false in the cases where it does not.
logic and truth conditions
Complex propositions are truth functions of elementary propositions. Logical operators alter truth conditions without naming extra objects in the world. A tautology is true under every assignment, and a contradiction is false under every assignment. Wittgenstein therefore treats both as lacking factual content while still belonging to the symbolism of logic.
Logic does not describe another layer of reality. Its form appears in the lawful use of signs. This is the basis of the book’s distinction between saying and showing.
saying and showing
Section 4.1212 states, “What can be shown cannot be said.” A proposition can state how things stand within the world. It cannot step outside every possible proposition and state the logical form that makes representation possible. That form is shown in meaningful symbolism.

Section 4.1212 states, “What can be shown cannot be said.” A proposition can state how things stand within the world. It cannot step outside every possible proposition and state the logical form that makes representation possible. That form is shown in meaningful symbolism.
The same limit shapes the closing discussion of value. Section 6.421 calls ethics transcendental. Ethical value, aesthetics, and the sense of the world do not appear as facts among other facts in the book’s system. Wittgenstein marks their importance by placing them outside factual speech.
the ladder
Section 6.54 compares the book’s own propositions to a ladder that a reader discards after climbing it. The final proposition follows: “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.” The ending creates a deliberate strain because the book uses propositions to clarify the limits of propositions.
The later Philosophical Investigations rejects the assumption that language has one underlying form. Read together, the change is visible. The Tractatus seeks the general structure of representation. The later work studies the different jobs words perform in ordinary practices.

Life has no pleasure higher or nobler than that of friendship. It is painful to consider that this sublime enjoyment may be impaired or destroyed by innumerable causes, and that there is no human possession of which the duration is less certain.
Many have talked, in very exalted language, of the perpetuity of friendship, of invincible constancy and unalienable kindness; and some examples have been seen of men who have continued faithful to their earliest choice, and whose affection has predominated over changes of fortune and contrariety of opinion.
But these instances are memorable because they are rare. The friendship which is to be practiced or expected by common mortals must take its rise from mutual pleasure and must end when the power ceases of delighting each other.
Many accidents therefore may happen by which the ardor of kindness will be abated, without criminal baseness or contemptible inconstancy on either part. To give pleasure is not always in our power; and little does he know himself who believes that he can be always able to receive it.
Those who would gladly pass their days together may be separated by the different course of their affairs; and friendship, like love, is destroyed by long absence, though it may be increased by short intermissions. What we have missed long enough to want it, we value more when it is regained; but that which has been lost till it is forgotten will be found at last with little gladness, and with still less if a substitute has supplied the place. A man deprived of the companion to whom he used to open his bosom, and with whom he shared the hours of leisure and merriment, feels the day at first hanging heavy on him; his difficulties oppress, and his doubts distract him; he sees time come and go without his wonted gratification, and all is sadness within and solitude about him. But this uneasiness never lasts long; necessity produces expedients, new amusements are discovered, and new conversation is admitted.

No expectation is more frequently disappointed than that which naturally arises in the mind from the prospect of meeting an old friend after long separation. We expect the attraction to be revived and the coalition to be renewed; no man considers how much alteration time has made in himself, and very few inquire what effect it has had upon others. The first hour convinces them that the pleasure, which they have formerly enjoyed, is forever at an end; different scenes have made different impressions; the opinions of both are changed; and that similitude of manners and sentiment is lost which confirmed them both in the approbation of themselves.
Friendship is often destroyed by opposition of interest, not only by the ponderous and visible interest which the desire of wealth and greatness forms and maintains but by a thousand secret and slight competitions, scarcely known to the mind upon which they operate. There is scarcely any man without some favorite trifle which he values above greater attainments, some desire of petty praise which he cannot patiently suffer to be frustrated. This minute ambition is sometimes crossed before it is known, and sometimes defeated by wanton petulance; but such attacks are seldom made without the loss of friendship; for whoever has once found the vulnerable part will always be feared, and the resentment will burn on in secret, of which shame hinders the discovery. This, however, is a slow malignity, which a wise man will obviate as inconsistent with quiet, and a good man will repress as contrary to virtue; but human happiness is sometimes violated by some more sudden strokes.
A dispute begun in jest upon a subject which, a moment before, was on both parts regarded with careless indifference is continued by the desire of conquest, till vanity kindles into rage, and opposition rankles into enmity. Against this hasty mischief, I know not what security can be obtained; men will be sometimes surprised into quarrels; and though they might both hasten to reconciliation, as soon as their tumult had subsided, yet two minds will seldom be found together which can at once subdue their discontent, or immediately enjoy the sweets of peace, without remembering the wounds of the conflict.

Friendship has other enemies. Suspicion is always hardening the cautious and disgust repelling the delicate. Very slender differences will sometimes part those whom long reciprocation of civility or beneficence has united. Lonelove and Ranger retired into the country to enjoy the company of each other and returned in six weeks cold and petulant; Ranger’s pleasure was to walk in the fields and Lonelove’s to sit in a bower; each had complied with the other in his turn, and each was angry that compliance had been exacted.
The most fatal disease of friendship is gradual decay, or dislike hourly increased by causes too slender for complaint and too numerous for removal. Those who are angry may be reconciled; those who have been injured may receive a recompense; but when the desire of pleasing and willingness to be pleased is silently diminished, the renovation of friendship is hopeless, as, when the vital powers sink into languor, there is no longer any use of the physician.
In real friendship the judgment, the genius, the prudence of each party become the common property of both.Maria Edgeworth, 1787

1.0 Ludwig Wittgenstein

1.01 Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (PDF) treats a proposition as a picture of a possible fact. Its saying/showing distinction marks what a factual proposition can state and what its logical form can only display.
1.02 Philosophical Investigations (PDF) follows words into language-games: giving orders, reporting, joking, praying. Use, training, rule-following, and correction give each practice its shape.



1.1 A.J. Ayer & Bertrand Russell.

1.11 Language, Truth and Logic by A. J. Ayer asks whether a proposition is analytic or open to empirical verification. The test is severe enough to make the status of ethical and metaphysical claims itself contentious.
1.12 On Denoting (1905) and Mathematical Logic as Based on the Theory of Types (1908) by Bertrand Russell ask how an expression works in a proposition when its grammatical form misleads us about its logical role.



1.2 Frank Ramsey

1.21 Truth and Probability (1926) connects degrees of belief to the odds a person would accept.
1.22 General Propositions and Causality (1929) calls belief “a map of neighbouring space by which we steer.” The 2025 notes extend that image: much of the map is water, and old beliefs leave marks after a revision.



1.3 The Cluster Structure of Thingspace⁠ by Eliezer Yudkowsky treats categories as clusters of correlated properties, a reason to examine a category’s predictive use instead of searching for its essence.


1.4 On Bounded Distrust by Zvi Mowshowitz asks what signal can still be extracted from a source whose distortions are known. Distrust has to be calibrated to the claim and context.


2.0 Albert Camus

2.01 The Myth of Sisyphus asks whether life is worth living once the demand for meaning meets an indifferent world. Its answer is revolt without an appeal to philosophical suicide.
2.02 The Rebel asks how refusal of injustice can remain committed to human limits, rather than license murder in the name of a promised future.
2.03 The First Man, the unfinished novel about childhood in colonial Algeria, returns the argument to poverty, family, and the search for an origin.

2.1 Gilles Deleuze

2.10 Nietzsche and Philosophy by Gilles Deleuze reads critique through the origin and value of values. This is the route into aesthetic value in the existing Nietzsche notes.
2.11 A Thousand Plateaus (PDF) by Deleuze and Félix Guattari develops rhizomes, assemblages, and multiplicities as ways to describe relations that do not grow from one root.



2.2 Being and Time (PDF) by Martin Heidegger starts from Dasein, already situated in a world of uses and concerns. Readiness-to-hand and presence-at-hand name two ways a thing becomes intelligible in that situation.


2.3 The Sickness unto Death by Søren Kierkegaard and The Need for Roots by Simone Weil hold a question open: what gives a self form when possibility multiplies? Hyperabundance makes that question practical, because chosen commitments need time and attention to become real.


3.0 A notebook and an essay do different work in a writing life.

3.01 On Keeping a Notebook by Joan Didion keeps contact with earlier selves. Its entries record how an event felt to the writer, even when they would make poor evidence for a factual diary.
3.02 The Age of the Essay and Writes and Write-Nots by Paul Graham treat an essay as an attempt (essayer): write a claim down, follow its consequences, and find out where thought is incomplete.

3.0 A notebook and an essay do different work in a writing life.

3.01 On Keeping a Notebook by Joan Didion keeps contact with earlier selves. Its entries record how an event felt to the writer, even when they would make poor evidence for a factual diary.
3.02 The Age of the Essay and Writes and Write-Nots by Paul Graham treat an essay as an attempt (essayer): write a claim down, follow its consequences, and find out where thought is incomplete.



3.1 Henrik Karlsson’s three essays make a sequence from private thought to public discovery to practical agency.

3.11 Writing to Think pins a vague claim to the page so that contradictions and counterexamples become visible. The friction is part of the method.
3.12 A Blog Post Is a Very Long and Complex Search Query treats specific public writing as a way to find people who can answer, challenge, or extend an unusual interest.
3.13 Agentic Fragments uses a reknitted sweater to show agency as seeing more degrees of freedom in an object, then acting on them. The public excerpt ends before the paid essay’s other fragments.



3.2 Impact, Agency, and Taste by Ben Kuhn separates choosing consequential work from carrying it through. Audience of One by Jasmine Sun belongs beside it as a prompt to examine whose judgment shapes taste and where the Overton Window enters the room.


3.3 The tools-for-thought track asks how a computer can extend a person’s working memory and agency.

3.31 As We May Think by Vannevar Bush imagines the memex and its associative trails; The Dream Machine by M. Mitchell Waldrop follows J. C. R. Licklider’s later vision of human-computer symbiosis.
3.32 Magic Ink by Bret Victor, Timeful Texts by Andy Matuschak and Michael Nielsen, and Tufte CSS give the page room for context, interaction, memory, and sidenotes.
3.33 File Over App by Steph Ango puts durable files under the owner’s control. Together these works explain the interest in personal computing and malleable software.



3.4 Universal Love, Said the Cactus Person by Scott Alexander belongs here because its demand for propositional proof interrupts an encounter. The 2025 notes use it to ask whether insisting on verification can turn a subject into an object.

4.0 Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (PDF) by Abelson and Sussman teaches procedures, data, and interpreters by constructing them, then changing the abstraction boundary.

4.01 The Art of Doing Science and Engineering by Richard Hamming makes sustained attention to important problems part of the craft.
4.02 How To Ask Questions The Smart Way by Eric S. Raymond asks for prior investigation and a precise account of the failure. Reading source code is often how a question becomes precise.



4.1 A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948) by Claude Shannon measures information against uncertainty in a distribution. On Exactitude in Science by Jorge Luis Borges supplies the counterimage of a map as large as its empire. Information theory, entropy, and compression matter because a useful representation leaves something out.


5.0 Cinema is a set of recurring questions about time, belonging, and what another person can teach us.

5.01 Past Lives (Celine Song) and Paris, Texas (Wim Wenders) return to lives that might have been and relationships altered by absence.
5.02 Good Will Hunting (Gus Van Sant) and Dead Poets Society (Peter Weir) put education, intimacy, and lived experience beside book knowledge.
5.03 La Haine (Mathieu Kassovitz) and The Defiant Ones (Stanley Kramer) put people in a social conflict they cannot think their way out of alone.
5.04 Tenet (Christopher Nolan) makes time itself the puzzle, then asks what an action means when cause and effect no longer arrive in their usual order.



5.1 Ma Gastronomie by Fernand Point and Marco Pierre White’s craft aphorisms keep cooking close to feeling, timing, and repeated practice. The practical version is a 3-quart Made In stainless clad saucier, Sunday uovo pasta, velouté, and atelier with friends.

My answers lead to moral objectivism.

Abstract Objects: Platonist

abstract ideas exist independently of human thought; numbers and shapes are discovered, not invented. see also Plato.


Aesthetic Beauty: Aesthetic Objectivist

some things are objectively beautiful or ugly; aesthetic disagreements have right and wrong answers. see also aesthetic value.


External World: External-world Realist

the external world exists and our senses convey accurate information about it; trust in sensory capabilities and science.


Free Will: Compatibilist

free will exists and is compatible with determinism; freedom means doing what you choose, even if choices are predetermined.


God: Atheist

confident that no supreme being exists; the idea of God’s existence is either absurd or demonstrably false.


Knowledge Claims: Contextualist

“knowledge” changes meaning based on context, stakes, and circumstances; no single consistent definition. see also Epistemology.


Laws of Nature: Anti-Humean

laws of nature exist objectively and dictate how events proceed; reject Hume’s view that causation is imaginary.


Meta-Ethics: Moral Realist

moral facts exist objectively, not relative to culture or person; some moral beliefs are objectively true or false. see also ethics.


Mind: Physicalist

the mind is physical, likely identical with or functionally realized by the brain; no belief in a soul.


Moral Judgment: Cognitivist

moral beliefs are about reality and can be true or false; moral judgments are meaningful statements about the world. see also ethics.


Newcomb’s Problem: One-Boxer

would choose only box A in Newcomb’s paradox, prioritizing predicted outcome over causal reasoning.


Normative Ethics: Deontologist

right and wrong determined by intentions, not consequences; good intentions make actions right. see also Philosophy and Kant.


Politics: Libertarian

strongly value individual freedom; governments should not interfere without strong reasons; enemy of paternalism.


Science: Scientific Realist

scientific theories approximately describe reality; unobservable entities like electrons exist because science says so.


Teletransporter: Leads to Survival

would use a teletransporter; destroying and recreating your body doesn’t kill you, just moves ‘you’. see also identity.


Truth: Deflationary Truth

truth has no metaphysical reality; “truth” is a useful logical tool but not an external reality.

This is 2023. A letter to myself. I will start with a mere nostalgic reflection filled with the goods and not so good, and ends with what I wish to accomplish for 2024.

To 2023 self,
Per tradition, your year began with a visit from your parents. We decided to do SF-NY, with good food, shopping, and visiting relatives. Living on a different continent, you’ve longed for the simple joys of home: those weekend returns, the comfort of a home-cooked meal, the tender gesture of cut fruits like in your younger days. Now, these moments are yearly reunions, where relatives journey across the globe. Despite finding these gatherings overwhelming, you cherish these visits.
It was in San Francisco that you found writing and reading, surrounded by a community of inspiring individuals. And it was San Francisco, that you and J crossed paths.
Running became a rhythmic solace amidst sleepless nights and turbulent thoughts. You would find yourself lacing up for a run, whether it was pushing through work until dawn or embarking on a 5-mile run along the Bay regardless of how tired you were. Running offered a sense of stability, a means to channel your energy and thoughts, though often at the expense of your physical and emotional health.
“You are young; you should be fine,” you would tell yourself, perhaps a bit too cavalierly.
Then came the spontaneous decision to go backpacking in Yosemite with S. Despite not being in the best shape, the allure of adventure was irresistible. It was a journey of firsts: your inaugural backpacking trip, your first visit to Yosemite, and your first encounter with the chill of near-freezing nights outdoors.
Yosemite

I don’t know about you, but the moment life hints at normalcy and tranquility, a restless itch starts to stir within me. It’s like K often says with a knowing smile, “you are a messy gyal.” There’s a peculiar comfort in chaos. Now, as I stand at this crossroads in the Bay Area, that restlessness is more pronounced than ever.
I had taken a leave from school to move to the Bay for work, a decision that now hung in the balance.
The Bay Area beckoned me to stay: doing what I love, being surrounded by friends, and those weekends with J. Yet, it was shadowed by the looming uncertainties of visa statuses.
The alternative, returning to Canada, is a retreat into a past that’s drenched in discomfort, into what I’ve always perceived as a life of constraints and unfulfilled potential. The very thought of leaving J, hitting pause on our shared dreams in San Francisco, sends a pang of sorrow through me. Canada is a return to a version of myself that I’ve struggled to leave behind. The visa challenges remained, no matter which border I call home.
In the quiet moments, your mind wrestled with these paths. “Stop, don’t leave. You can do it. Stay,” a voice within you whispered, a blend of hope and desperation. It was a plea to cling to the life you’ve started to build here.
It was a Sunday afternoon, you and J were enjoying a cup of coffee, in the Marina. Like whispers of the gentlest breeze, the wind danced through J’s hair, each strand a melody, weaving tales of love in the air. It carried J’s scent, a tapestry of rose subtly entwined with earth’s warm embrace, a tender symphony barely touching the senses. You whispered in her ears, “I have to leave for Toronto.” Her hair, once a playground for your fingers, now swayed to the rhythm of a compassionate wind, each strand moving with the grace of unshed tears. The air, perfumed with the delicate scent of roses and spices, seemed to hold our memories, cradling them gently as if to soften the blow of parting.

Our eyes met, yet tinged with the inevitable sorrow of farewell. Words were unnecessary; our hearts spoke in silent verses, each beat a soft adieu. It was a parting not of anger or regret, but of two souls acknowledging their journey together had reached a tender, inevitable end. We both sit there, cried in silent.
The gentle wind, a compassionate witness to our farewell, carried away the last whispers of a love that was as beautiful as it was ephemeral, leaving behind a calm, poignant tranquility.

It was now sunny July, you found yourself back in Canada, slowly acclimating to the new life. The makeshift bed, consists of two fitted sheets, a duvet, and a pillow, while waiting for furnitures to arrive back from SF, offered a modest comfort yet lacked the essence of home.
This wasn’t your first rodeo. Relocations has somewhat become normalcy for you: leaving Hanoi for boarding school seven years ago, then moving across Canada for university and lived in campus housing, to moving into student housing, alone amidst 2020’s misfortunes, returning to Vietnam shortly after, then moved back to Canada for online-university living in an overcrowded unhygienic household filled with strangers, followed by your determination to leave Canada once and for all to SF, to chase the “American dream”. However, this time, the feeling stirred differently. Gone was the wide-eyed public school kid who first stepped onto Canadian soil, filled with aspirations. Faded, too, was the image of the bewildered freshman adrift in a sea of unfamiliar faces at university. And the weary, drained engineer who sought refuge in San Francisco, seeking an escape, had evolved.
Now, as you sat amidst the quiet of your new space, you grappled with a curious blend of familiarity and foreignness.

In the company of books, you sought refuge. You also rekindled old friendships, those that had lain dormant in the wake of your sojourn to San Francisco.
There was a sense of quiet accomplishment in the transformation of your apartment, a life being patiently rebuilt, piece by piece. Physical exertion, too, found its place in your routine: climbing gym, the disciplined rhythm of your runs. The runs, though lacking the scenic vistas of San Francisco, offered a more introspective landscape.
Work, too, assumed a new significance with projects, OpenLLM. It demanded of you a pace and a depth of understanding that was both exhilarating and daunting. Then there was HackTheNorth. Convincing S to sponsor HackTheNorth, and your subsequent workshop on language models, was a reconnection to a belief in hacker culture, filled with anticipation and excitement for building technology.
HackTheNorth 2023, with BentoML

Homecooked meals for some of the functions with friends
You showed up. You showed your love and affection for your friends through home-cooked meals. Potlucks, tasting menus: they were your ways of nurturing the bonds of friendship, a respite from the pressures of student life.
Remember that Halloween, when you cooked a feast, ensuring your friends were well-fed and ready for a night of revelry? Surrounded by the sizzling skillet and steaming hot mashed potatoes, you found a sense of belonging. You’ve never seen yourself as the quintessential party-goer, often feeling like an observer on the fringes of the festivities. But you went, even as a part of you remained reluctant.
At the party, a familiar sensation crept in: a detachment from the scene around you. You didn’t quite mesh with this crowd. This realisation triggered a rush of anxiety, urging you to escape.
So, you left. You left the noise, the laughter, and returned to the silence of your home. There you were greeted by the remnants of your cooking: the pots, pans, and utensils from the meal.
In the stillness of your kitchen, loneliness enveloped you. You sat there, amidst the pans, and tears began to fall.

Remember that breakup with J? The summer was heartbreak and restless nights. It’s funny how we try to mend ourselves, isn’t it? With a schedule as a plaster over a gaping wound. I had it all mapped out, or so I thought.
It was on a nondescript day, November 13th, that I found myself on a date with a woman I’d met online. The evening was unremarkable, tinged with the effort of trying to reconnect with the world. We ended up at her place, an encounter that was at best, mediocre. In the midst of the intimacy, memories of J invaded my mind, unbidden.
J and I, we were polyamorous. Unorthodox, yes (but not really in SF), but to each other, we were anchors. My reluctance to move back to Canada was rooted in her: she was my ‘it’, my endgame. And then a message from J pierced the night. Her words, simple yet loaded, unravelled me.
We had agreed to silence, to give time and space for healing. But there I was, haunted by the love that embraced my most authentic self, the part of me unshielded by the armor I’d forged over the years. That night was restless, the presence of another unable to fill the void. 3:30 am, my phone shattered the silence: it was J. Panic and longing intertwined as I answered. What harm could there be?
What followed were late-night conversations, spanning many weeks. J’s voice, laced with tears, spoke of longing and loss. Our talks were a roller-coaster: laughter quickly drowned by arguments, smiles eclipsed by sorrow. I was a cocktail of anger and sadness; I had moved on, or so I had convinced myself. Why now, in the midst of this? J’s behaviour was a mystery, a deviation from her usual sensibility. And there I lay, sleep eluding me, troubled by the thought of her distress.
One morning, you found yourself seeking refuge in the kitchen. There’s a certain healing power in cooking: the methodical chopping of vegetables, the hiss of ingredients in the skillet. But even there, the spectre of J haunted you.

One morning, you found yourself seeking refuge in the kitchen. There’s a certain healing power in cooking: the methodical chopping of vegetables, the hiss of ingredients in the skillet. But even there, the spectre of J haunted you.
A momentary lapse in attention brought a sharp pain. A drop of blood bloomed on the cutting board. The sight of it, coupled with the realisation that you had cut your finger, brought a wave of lightheadedness. Yet, even as the shock set in, you instinctively reached for a towel, pressing it firmly against the wound. You navigated your way to the first-aid kit. Your hands worked to clean and dress the wound.
After tending to the injury, you slumped against the fridge, your gaze drifting aimlessly to the ceiling. In an instant, a thought flickered through your mind: the notion of ending it all. But just as quickly as it surfaced, it dissipated at the thought of your mother. The image of her, perhaps unaware of the depths of your current struggles, yet invariably intertwined with your existence, acted as a grounding force. In the quiet of your kitchen, with the pain in your finger a sharp but grounding sensation, you were left to confront your ‘ego’: the pain, the emotion, the longing, the love, and the will to endure.

Navigating the aftermath of a first serious relationship is hard, especially for someone who had always embraced solitude. When it ended, I was overwhelmed like a teacup caught in a relentless downpour.
J was a mirror to parts of myself I hadn’t known. But as the emotional turbulence continued, my logical self, long subdued, finally asserted itself. It whispered of the need for closure, for the sake of my own well-being. The final call to J was a necessary severance, blocking all lines of communication going forward.
This decision, difficult as it was, felt like the only way forward, a path to healing for both of you. Sharing experiences with Mom did lift a weight off your shoulders.
It marked a turning point, a chance to truly move on. And before you knew it, Christmas break was upon you.
Your return to school was marked by a fresh perspective, one shaped by your stint in SF. School is now a place for you to explore your interests and have the joy of learning, as it should be. For the first time, you found joy in the very structure of academia.

Dasein exists in relations to other being, as “the ‘essence’ of Dasein lies in its existence.”1 We wake up each day, startled by our own presence. We spend our nights harboring dreams that might startle us awake.

But what does it mean to truly be there in an age when “there” has become everywhere and nowhere?
When presence splits between pixels and flesh, between midnight texts and morning coffee?

8. books and reading that constitutes to character-building.

8.1 Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus by Ludwig Wittgenstein. I like the structure of the book and stole it for this document, as well as the permission to shut up about love.

wittgenstein’s ladder: you climb propositions until the propositions dissolve. what remains is the mystical that “makes itself manifest” (6.522). he told ludwig von ficker, whom he hoped would publish it (1919), that the book’s point was ethical: “i have managed in my book to put everything firmly into place by being silent about it.”
the limits of my language mean the limits of my world (5.6). this explained why N couldn’t fit inside english grammatical structures (2.02).
liberation from the compulsion to articulate everything. the unsayable is not the meaningless.


8.2 The Gay Science by Friedrich Nietzsche. I like to think of the eternal recurrence as attention-practice.

if a demon told you this life would repeat infinitely (the grief, the work half-finished, the L who left) would you curse him or call it divine? Nietzsche uses this as litmus test for life-affirmation.
amor fati: “i want to learn more and more to see as beautiful what is necessary in things” (§276). acceptance as wanting-what-is so completely that you’d will its eternal return.
can i affirm this year as it actually is? the question became a daily weighting-updating function. “only great pain is the ultimate liberator of the spirit.”

8.3 Waiting for God by Simone Weil. Makes me wrestle with the concept of big-capital-G man and omnipotence paradox.

“absolutely unmixed attention is prayer” (this line is from Gravity and Grace, not Waiting for God). active receptivity: waiting for reality to disclose itself rather than forcing disclosure.
“the love of our neighbor in all its fullness simply means being able to say to him: ‘what are you going through?’” this reframed what i owed N, what i owed L.
she claims any discipline (even kernel development) prepares the soul for encounter. “every school exercise, thought of in this way, is like a sacrament.” i take her seriously.


8.4 Letters to Milena by Franz Kafka. He showed me what happens when transmission fails.

“writing letters means exposing oneself to the ghosts, who are greedily waiting for precisely that. written kisses never arrive at their destination; the ghosts drink them up on the way.”
a confession meant as appreciation transforms, by the act of sending, into something that cannot be taken back. the letter drifts into the void. you watch three bubbles appear and disappear.
“you are the knife i turn inside myself; that is love.” the intensity of desire becomes the obstacle. my letters to L were this, the very writing a form of turning.


8.5 Crime and Punishment by Fyodor Dostoevsky demonstrated what raskolnikov got wrong.

his theory: extraordinary men have inner right to transgress moral law. the novel’s argument: such theories collapse on contact with embodied existence. you cannot think your way past guilt.
sonya sees raskolnikov fully: knows his crime, attends anyway. non-judgmental without excusing. this is the counter-principle to rationalist ethics: love operates through presence.
raskolnikov’s crime stems from failure of attention: he constituted the pawnbroker as “louse” rather than person. ivan karamazov (in The Brothers Karamazov) can love humanity only at a distance, never the neighbor in front of him. the universal requires the concrete.

ethical commitment creates conditions for depth: attending to the same person across time, seeing them ever more deeply. maybe time to concentrate (2.5).

8.9 the vibe-list of essays that I particularly enjoyed this year:

Radical Fun by Ava: fun is fundamentally about connection, and friendship is the primary gateway to meaningful fun. fun is a skill requiring intentional cultivation. love for friends is as serious as romantic love, requiring “time, patience, repetition and yearning.” this is the friendship theory of everything: love for friends using the same circuitry.
Presence by Human Invariant: physical presence exposes the “illegible” aspects of people and knowledge that cannot be transmitted through polished online work products. the ability and desire to care is built through presence. “the real updates to your life don’t come from reading words online.” your true friends are those willing to cross bridges to see you.
Please Don’t Throw Your Mind Away⁠ on LessWrong: warns against suppressing “playful thinking” in favor of urgent, goal-directed productivity. when people arrive at the x-risk community, they feel pressure to orient everything around backchained goals, causing them to throw away natural curiosity. meaning cannot be fully derived from external goals; some must emerge from letting the mind follow its own interests.
Productivity by Alexey Guzey: all productivity systems eventually break down; the goal should be creating sustainable rhythms rather than fighting impulses. novel locations temporarily restore rule-following ability. productivity should emerge from alignment between what you want and what you do.
Why Have Sex by Offhand Quibbles: complicates the simple-pleasure model of intimacy. in the same register as ava’s friendship piece: the things that matter require skill and sustained engagement.
A Constellation of Lookers by Henrik Karlsson: local artists who spent their lives looking intensely at their landscape form a “constellation” connected by their shared need to contemplate their lifeworld, though they never knew each other. those who attend deeply to reality may feel alone but are secretly part of a pattern visible across time.

I have always cared too much for people, in the messy, overwhelming way that children learn to love: by watching, by receiving, by doing. My parents showed love through abundance: extra dumplings in the soup, a fourth serving of rice, endless variations of the same dish until they got it exactly how I liked it.
I tried, for years, to rationalise love into neat equations. If I cook this meal, if I show up at this time, if I remember these details, then surely the output would be connection, would be friendship, would be love. But love resists these algorithms. Food became my bridge across this gap between rational thought and emotional truth. When I cook for someone, I’m saying what I cannot calculate: here is my time, my attention, my care rendered into something you can taste.
In a sense, each meal is a promise: I will nourish you, and in return, we will share this moment.
The exchange rate is impossible to quantify. How many hours of chopping vegetables equals one genuine laugh? How many carefully seasoned dishes equals one moment of true understanding?
Simone Weil wrote that “attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.”1 When I cook for you, I’m not trying to solve for x anymore. I’m simply saying: I see you. I care about you, deeply.

Hi Anthony,
We met this year, for real, like really hang out. That’s the strange part: it feels like longer. Ours arrived compressed: from twitter convos to a few conversations and suddenly I had a dialectic partner, someone who could take the half-formed thought I was circling and show me its structure from an angle I couldn’t see. Most conversations are parallel monologues. Somehow ours collides (maybe due to shared interests in ml).
Hegel had this concept, aufhebung, usually translated “sublation” and often flattened into “synthesis”, which means something closer to “preservation through transcendence.” When two positions meet and genuinely engage, the result is the elevation to a plane where both are true in a transformed sense. That’s how I feel about our conversations. I often come in with an absurd/ridiculous position, you come in with yours, and what we leave with belongs to neither of us.
The bud disappears when the blossom breaks through, and we might say that the former is refuted by the latter [...] But the ceaseless activity of their own inherent nature makes them at the same time moments of an organic unity, where they not merely do not contradict one another, but where one is as necessary as the other.Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit, preface (Baillie translation, 1910)

The reels you send me (Žižek’s meme rambling about ideology/love, Hegel clips with zoomer edits) are entertainment (brainrot go brrr) and also a kind of shared vocabulary. Žižek uses jokes and pop culture because they reveal the structure of ideology through its failures. We do something similar, I think. We use memes and fragments and late-night riffs to triangulate toward something neither of us could articulate directly.
The nights at Reservoir have this quality. Jazz in the background, conversation that wanders but somehow always lands somewhere real. We talk ML without the tech-bro energy. The field is saturated with people who’ve optimized the performance of caring about alignment while actually caring about status and funding. You haven’t fallen into the traps of the “vibecoders-maxxing” and “oh-look-at-my-92b-tokens-generated-with-cursor-wrapped” bros. You’re just trying to figure out what’s true, and what works, which means you’re willing to be wrong, which means the conversation can actually go somewhere.

The alignment debates that we occasionally get into (orthogonality, instrumental convergence, value specification, emergent misalignment) are the live wires of the next few decades, albeit somewhat obtuse, for sure. Bostrom’s orthogonality thesis says intelligence and goals are independent: you can have arbitrarily high capability pursuing arbitrarily misaligned objectives.1 And instrumental convergence means any sufficiently intelligent system, regardless of terminal goals, will converge on certain instrumental subgoals, like self-preservation and resource acquisition, because surviving is useful for achieving whatever it does want.
These are the kinds of problems where having a thinking partner matters. Stuart Russell’s point is that we can’t fully specify human values because we don’t fully know them.2 The alignment problem is ultimately about pointing at something we cannot describe. That is partly a philosophical problem, and philosophical problems require dialogue. They require someone who can see the shape of your confusion from outside it.
Genuine refutation must penetrate the opponent's stronghold and meet him on his own ground; no advantage is gained by attacking him somewhere else and defeating him where he is not.Hegel, Science of Logic, book III

What I value about our friendship is the absence of performance. We’re trying to figure out what’s there, which requires being willing to say the dumb thing and admit when the position you were defending three minutes ago now seems wrong. Žižek be like: the point is to raise the contradiction to the level of the concept, to grasp its necessity.3 We don’t necessarily resolve our disagreements but come to an understanding why they’re necessary given how we’re each positioned.
I’m glad our paths crossed this year. The whole discourse around where ML is headed is easy to get lost in. Having someone to think with, someone whose refutations feel like gifts, makes it somewhat more breathable.
More nights at Reservoir. More reels. More aufhebung in practice: two positions becoming a third thing that belongs to neither of us but couldn’t exist without both.

Hi Cairo,
I remember what it felt like. the airport, the paperwork, the particular silence of arriving somewhere that doesn’t know your name yet. i did it years ago: vietnam to canada, a teenager with a suitcase and a student visa and no real sense of what i was trading away. you did it this year. you packed a life into boxes and bet on yourself, and i watched from the other side of the screen, recognizing the shape of the thing even if the details were different.
There’s an immigrant’s arithmetic nobody warns you about. you leave your whole life back in Australia, and you trade a thousand small certainties for a handful of high-upside possibilities. the corner store that knew your order. the friends you could call without planning. the way your own vernacular and slang sat easy in your mouth, unremarkable, just there. you pay for every future friendship with a present loneliness. you buy a new life with a temporary loss of fluency in the invisible rules that make a day feel easy instead of expensive.
Edward Said wrote about exile as a “discontinuous state of being”: the self before and the self after, with a break between them that never fully heals1. i think that’s too dramatic for most of us. what i felt, and what i imagine you’re feeling, is something quieter: a thinning. the old life doesn’t disappear. it keeps running in the background threads, just harder to touch. you carry it like a photograph in a wallet, still yours, but flattened into something you look at instead of live inside.
To a wise man, the whole earth is open; for the native land of a good soul is the whole earth.Democritus, fragment 68 B247 (Diels–Kranz)
That line sounds noble until you’re actually doing it. the whole earth is open, sure, but belonging takes time. it takes the slow accumulation of references only locals understand, the moment when you stop translating in your head and just speak. you’re in the early phase of that accumulation now, and i want you to know: it compounds. the first year is the hardest. then one day you realize you’ve built something real without noticing the exact moment it became real.

From what i can tell, you’re doing well, in the sense of someone who is actually building. finding routines. finding people. learning a new place the way you learn a language, through the slow replacement of confusion with familiarity. that early phase, where every errand is research and every conversation costs extra attention, is its own form of work. the kind that doesn’t photograph well.
there’s a specific kind of strength in being a stranger and staying kind anyway. it would be easy to turn sharp, to treat the new place as hostile territory you’re just trying to survive. you didn’t do that. you stayed open even when openness was expensive. i noticed that, and i respect it.
Sebald’s emigrants are never quite at home, never quite foreign2. i don’t think it has to be that melancholy. some of us find a way to make the in-between feel like a place worth living. you seem to be doing that.

if you need anything (someone to just sit on the phone while you pace around your apartment at 2am because the time zones don’t line up with anyone else) i’m here. distance is just latency. you don’t have to do the whole thing alone, even when it feels like you do.
i know the weight of a suitcase. i know the weight of a dream that pulls you somewhere new. i’m glad you’re carrying both.

The cord brought us closer this year. That sentence sounds so obviously digital-age that it almost embarrasses me to write it, but there’s no other way to say it honestly. We met through Discord servers: mutual friends, overlapping interests. And then, over months of messages and voice calls and the ambient awareness of each other’s presence, something accumulated that I’d have to call friendship.
McLuhan’s line about the medium being the message gets quoted so often it’s almost lost its meaning, but I think about it whenever I try to explain how online relationships work to people who haven’t had them.1 Text flattens tone but preserves exactness. Voice adds warmth but disappears the moment it’s spoken. The rhythm of when someone shows up (which threads they join, which they ignore, how long they take to respond) becomes its own form of communication. You learn someone through the gaps between messages as much as the messages themselves.
What’s funny is how “online” all of this sounds, and how unavoidably real it becomes anyway. Sherry Turkle wrote about digital connection as a thin substitute for the real thing, “alone together.”2 I don’t think that’s wrong, exactly. Some online friendships stay thin. Others don’t. The difference, I think, is whether people are willing to be awkward and show up even when there’s nothing clever to contribute. You do that consistently.

What I respect most is how you carry yourself in a chat. Your tone doesn’t drift into the cheap cynicism that’s basically the default register of the internet. You don’t treat conversation like a game of status, where every message is really about positioning. You say what you think, and you listen to what other people think.
And when you do talk about things you care about, it lands differently than most people’s opinions: less “here’s my take,” more “here’s what survived contact with reality.” You can tell the thinking happened before the speaking, that you’re reporting back from somewhere you’ve already been. Hi Jesse,
Another year of dental school. Another year of you doing the thing: the grind, the exams, the clinics, the everything. You already know. But I’m going to say it anyway.
Last year I wrote about our late-night conversations, the endless riffing on what it means to be a man in this particular moment of history. We quoted Marcus Aurelius at each other like a secret handshake. This year, those conversations deepened. We talked about relationships in the specific way people talk when they’re actually in it, when the stakes are real and the questions don’t have clean answers. The Hinge stream, and the late talks.
Accept the things to which fate binds you, and love the people with whom fate brings you together, but do so with all your heart.Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.39 (popular rendering)
That line hits differently when you’re actually trying to do it.1 Loving with all your heart sounds simple until you realize it requires choosing, and the daily discipline of attention and repair.

Alain de Botton argues for a philosophy of pessimism about love.2 The romantic myth tells us we have to find the right person, and everything will work out. Compatibility is something you discover. Botton says that’s backwards: “Compatibility is an achievement of love; it must not be its precondition.” You make yourselves compatible through the slow, unglamorous work of understanding each other and repairing ruptures. The work never ends.
In The Course of Love he writes: “pronouncing a lover ‘perfect’ can only be a sign that we have failed to understand them.” Real love begins after the illusion breaks, after you see the person clearly and choose them anyway, because you’ve decided that this is the imperfection you’re willing to work with.
Rilke puts it differently, but he’s circling the same thing:
Love consists in this, that two solitudes protect and touch and greet each other.Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet, letter 7 (1904)
Two solitudes. The romantic myth says you’re incomplete until someone completes you. Rilke is more/less emphasizing that you have to be whole first. You have to be a solitude worth protecting. And then love becomes two complete people meeting, each standing guard over the other’s separateness.

I think about our conversations on what it means to be a man, and I realize we were really talking about this. The stoics were against being captured by emotion, letting circumstance dictate your inner state. Marcus Aurelius wrote lovingly about his wife. Seneca’s letters are full of tenderness. The point was to make love something you do.
bell hooks says it bluntly: thinking of love “as an action rather than a feeling” is how anyone using the word “automatically assumes accountability and responsibility.”3 That’s the stoic insight translated into relationship terms. It’s the same discipline you bring to dental school: showing up when you don’t feel like it, doing the reps.
For one human being to love another human being: that is perhaps the most difficult task that has been entrusted to us, the ultimate task, the final test and proof.Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet, letter 7 (Stephen Mitchell translation)

I’m proud of who you’re becoming. The dental school grind is shaping you, yes, but so are the relationship convos where we try to figure out what it means to love well. You’re doing the reps. That’s all any of us can do.
I’m here whenever you need me. In the real way: if something breaks, if you’re exhausted, if you need to talk through a relationship problem at 2am. You don’t need an occasion to reach out. I don’t need one to pick up.
You know where to find me.

Hi Parth,
Heidegger makes a distinction between Zuhandenheit (the ready-to-hand) and Vorhandenheit, the present-at-hand. That these are opposites seems clear, but a moment of reflection on something like a hammer is instructive: If all goes well, the hammer disappears from your awareness, but if it breaks or otherwise stops doing what it’s supposed to, it takes center stage for a while until it is somehow repaired or replaced. So infrastructure that does its job quietly disappears from our radar, while bad infrastructure makes us pay constant attention, to work around its problems, and to constantly re-jig our plans against the irregularities that it forces on us. In that sense, toolmaking is a craft whose goal is to make things disappear; to allow them to be in a state of Zuhandenheit as much as possible.
These thoughts were brought to mind by running a few models locally with ollama run. While I’ve written some words about these models, the hidden stack that actually delivers those words (quantization decisions, memory management, inference optimization, and so much more) is completely out of sight. The great thing is that it works, that the complexity is withdrawn so all I have to think about is models and their use. One could think of this as a kind of failure of attention. To some extent, perhaps it is, but there’s also something very good about being able to work with the models directly without constantly battling with their inner machinery.
Consider the case of my work on inference. Prefill is essentially compute-bound while decode is memory-bandwidth bound. Memory bandwidth is the central bottleneck in the whole system, and one should be able to see the effects of various tradeoffs (better but more memory-intensive models, vocab sizes, and so on) in it. When your task is to take a load of compute capabilities and memory bandwidth and stick them in a box and make sure the result is a piece of software that people can use, you spend a lot of time thinking about how to avoid exceeding a memory bandwidth bottleneck and then how to keep the result from choking on that limit while also handling the rest of the work. You spend a lot of time trying until the model runs fast, or you have to conclude it can’t.

To be very clear, I have made a lot of mistakes and find the process hard and challenging. Every day, I am considerably less able to organize my obsession into a coherent plan than I was as a kid.
But I can’t help thinking it’s impressive, perhaps admirable, that you have remained so closely involved with the material work of building something real from metal and silicon. And to have a strong taste for technical depth without flailing. One of our strongest values is evidenced by willingness to actually think through a problem to its conclusion rather than by bravado and performative problem-solving.
Thank you for going the distance and, yes, keep building.

The sidewalk exhales noon: heat‑plumes writhe
like slow dragons under iron lids.

ghosts across the wall, half‑smiled, half‑gone.

permanently mid‑flight, never free.

a subtitle for change we can’t read.

like late‑October river ice.

arrives first. Between us:
two espresso martinis, the quiet fact
of your empty Monday mornings.

  Spreadsheet-sized.

no hollow suit to be tried on,
no doll sewn shut for want or need,
no rubber heart for mouths to feed.

Let contracts burn. You wear no disguise.

the map your courage etches there.

Red-gold surrender. Drifting down
to nurse the soil. That’s how you fall:
  to
    root again.

I’ve been watching trees, how they know
to let go when holding on
becomes the heavier burden. Just seasons
doing what they do.

of belonging Monday through Friday.

with something unquantifiable. Call it
presence. The thing that makes
strangers turn, lean in, remember
why they came.

Even in this wrong season, they fall
with specific grace. Passing
through the compartmentalized day.
