So far, I’ve lived on my own (or far away from family) for a third of my life, having made the leap to Canada at 16. This move, though seemingly late compared to my high school peers, was a turning point.
In the years before my departure, I was enrolled at Hanoi-Amsterdam⁠, which some consider the “crème de la crème” school within the public school system in Vietnam. Middle school was pretty much an endless march of memorisation and night classes, all leading up to the high school entrance exams. Within this rigorous routine, there was no room for complaints or questions. I wasn’t content, yet I found a way to push through, not realising the toll it was taking on my mental and physical health. Therapy, attempted much later, didn’t reveal anything new. Perhaps my continued sessions are a search for the external validation that I’ve longed for. My sense of self was intertwined with being accepted into this institution.

Three weeks before the entrance exam, or something like that. Saturday afternoon.
The sun blazed down from an afternoon sky devoid of clouds. Inside, within the four walls of the room where I had spent my years growing from a child into something resembling an adult, I sat hunched over my literature review. The task was simple in theory: memorize one of three essential poems. Yet, as the sunlight fought its way through the window, the words seemed to dance and dodge my grasp.
My focus was a blade, dulling with each failed attempt to carve the verses into my memory. The stillness of the room was punctuated only by the occasional creak of the house settling. The air was thick, the kind of heat that makes the mind sluggish, the body weary.
Frustration mounted. I pressed on, the words of the poem blurring before my eyes. My mom, ever attuned to my struggles, sensed my distress. Her suggestion to move on was gentle, her words soft, “It’s okay, darling, let’s skip this one.” But to me, they sounded like a verdict, a confirmation of my fears.
At 15, her words did not offer the comfort she intended. Tears streamed down my face.
  Mom, I can't fail this exam.
I managed through sobs, the words thick in my throat.

Even after securing my place at Hanoi-Amsterdam, my disdain for it grew. The competitive and toxic atmosphere was a far cry from what I expected. It was a battleground for status, with little regard for collaboration or personal growth. My mom, herself an educator, saw the system’s failure to nurture curiosity or critical thinking. So, when the chance to study abroad presented itself, I seized it, leaving Vietnam behind.
The transition from the rigid, rote-learning environment to the more open, discussion-based system in Canada was jarring. The shift from a public school to a private boarding school was equally disorienting. I was completely baffled, destroyed, was up to no good (if you knew me you knew what I’m talking about!). But one thing that I have learnt from all the trauma accumulated throughout my experience at Amsterdam was that “Mama ain’t raised no quitter.” Thus, a not-quite-okay-but-found-a-functional-way-to-survive mental model persisted throughout high school. Then the rest was history.

The world is a scary place, but I’m learning to cope through it.

Writing it down felt like opening a door I have long left shut. I had neatly folded the memory away, not realising how much it still pulsed beneath the surface. It’s one thing to carry your past quietly within you, another entirely to lay it out for the world (and yourself) to see.
Equanimity, that state of calm balance, feels elusive, almost mythical, when you’ve lived with chaos so intimately. There’s a fear in tranquility, a suspicion of its silence. What does it mean to be at peace when you’ve grown accustomed to the noise?

Last but not least, I would leave you, future Aaron, with a few questions that past-Aaron has longed to answer, in a kind of Socratic dialogue:
Q: who are you trying to become?
A: Perhaps it is less about becoming and more about unravelling the complexities from within. There is a certain naive desire, a childlike curiosity, that propels me towards the unknown. At the moment, I’m trying to protect that child and shield him from the turbulence and chaos we call life.
Q: why can’t you move back home?
A: Consider the river and the dam. The river meanders, shaped by the land it traverses, until it reaches the dam. Here, it lies in a deep réservoir, a body of water in waiting, destined to flow through turbines and continue its journey downstream. The sun draws the water skyward, and it returns as rain, nourishing the earth on its way back to the river. But the droplets that return are transformed, no longer the same entities that once rested in the dam’s embrace.
Leaving one’s home for foreign shores is such a journey. When one leaves home, they embark on a trajectory vastly different from those who stay. The familiar becomes distant, and upon return, the once-known world feels alien. You stand apart, changed in the eyes of those who remember who you once were. “Home” remains a memory preserved in amber, while you, like the river, have been irrevocably altered by your experiences. In other words, this is often known as the theme of displacement
To return home is to face a paradox: the physical space may be unchanged, the same faces may greet you, the house of your childhood may still nestle in its familiar spot, but your perception of it all has shifted, and the person they remember is gone.

A: I want to achieve a sense of peace, a balance between the chaos and the stillness, and to learn to let people in. I want to look back on what we have gone through, the stillness, the moments of joy and sorrow, and know that I have lived fully. Question 

A voice turned Socrates away from politics. Wisely, as Socrates sees it. “Do you really imagine I could have survived all these years, if I had led a public life?” (42) You cannot serve both justice and the state. “He who will fight for the right, if he would live even for a brief space, must have a private station and not a public one”—that is, must lead a private, not a public life, if he is to survive. (41)

Why does Socrates say this? What reasons can you find (whether in Apology or elsewhere) for his position? Summarise and explain in your own words.
Is the idea one you find plausible or implausible? Explain why you take your view.

In Plato’s Apology, Socrates draws a boundary between pursuing a life of justice and engaging in politics. He holds that a life devoted to righteousness is at odds with political office: “He who will fight for the right, if he would live even for a brief space, must have a private station and not a public one” (32a). Socrates gives two reasons for this, one about survival and one about service. I find the first persuasive for Athens and implausible as a general rule, and the second is what keeps his position from being the selfish withdrawal it can look like.
Socrates first ascribes his abstention to a divine sign, “a kind of voice” that “always forbids but never commands” and “deters me from being a politician” (31d). He then gives the sign a reason he endorses: “if I had engaged in politics, I should have perished long ago, and done no good either to you or to myself” (31d-e). The reason is general. No man who honestly opposes “the many lawless and unrighteous deeds which are done in a state” will save his life (31e). The Athenian assembly decided by majority, and a citizen who stood against the majority in a public role stood against the body that could put him to death.
He has evidence from his own life, and the two episodes are what make his rhetorical question, “Do you really imagine I could have survived all these years, if I had led a public life?” (32e), more than a guess. The one time he held office, as a member of the Council in 406 BC, he alone opposed the illegal collective trial of the generals after Arginusae, while the orators threatened to impeach and arrest him (32b-c). Under the Thirty, he was ordered with four others to arrest Leon of Salamis for execution and went home instead; he says he would probably have been killed for it if the Thirty had not fallen soon after (32c-d). In both cases, holding a public role put him where he had to choose between doing injustice and dying.

His mission comes from a different source. Socrates recounts the Oracle at Delphi’s answer that “no man [is] wiser” than he, and his attempt to refute it by questioning those reputed wise. None could give satisfactory answers, which led him to see that his wisdom lay in recognising his own ignorance (21a-23b). He took up the task of urging others to examine their lives (23b-c), summed up in “the unexamined life is not worth living” (38a). Because “injustice and disobedience to a better, whether God or man, is evil and dishonourable” (29b), and because doing injustice harms the soul of the one who does it, he would rather die than compromise (30b-c, 38e-39b). His trial shows this: he would not retract his philosophy to save himself.
The second reason answers the charge that this is selfish. Socrates claims his private questioning is the greatest service he can do the city. He is the gadfly that the god attached to Athens, “a great and noble steed who is tardy in his motions owing to his very size,” to rouse it (30e), and he spent his life going to each citizen privately to persuade them to care for virtue before possessions (36c). On his account the private station is a public service carried out one conversation at a time, and it is the only kind he could keep doing without being killed.
I find the survival claim plausible for Athens and implausible as a rule. It depends on institutions in which the majority could execute a dissenter, as it finally did him. Constitutional states built term limits, independent courts and protections for dissent largely so that a person can oppose the majority from a public role without dying for it. Socrates’ own record also cuts against a strict separation. He did hold office, and his two refusals are acts of a public life lived with integrity; he survived the second by the luck of the Thirty’s fall. What his record shows is that office raises the price of integrity, not that the two are incompatible.

The gadfly argument is stronger, but it measures success by the souls improved and the integrity kept, not by what changes in the city’s laws. Martin Luther King Jr. cites Socrates twice in the Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963) as his model of creative tension and civil disobedience (Strauss). King held no office either, but he took the gadfly’s questioning into the street and aimed it at the law, and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlived him. His assassination in 1968 is a reminder that Socrates’ warning about survival was not wrong. It also shows the gadfly can work through politics rather than beside it.
Plato’s Apology makes a persuasive case that a just person in Athens’ public life risked death, and that private questioning can serve the city. It does not show that withdrawal from political life is the only path for a philosopher who wants to keep their integrity. A life worth living, on my view, balances moral integrity with political engagement, and Socrates’ own life, the Council seat and the refusal under the Thirty included, is closer to that balance than his conclusion admits.

Question 

With a view to action, experience seems in no respect inferior to art [i.e., technical knowledge, e.g., engineering or medicine], and men of experience succeed even better than those who have theory without experience… But yet we think that knowledge and understanding belong to art [i.e., technical mastery] rather than to experience, and we suppose artists [i.e., technicians, engineers] to be wiser than men of experience… [W]e do not regard any of the senses as wisdom; yet surely these give the most authoritative knowledge of particulars. (132)
Here Aristotle says people with experience only do not have knowledge, do not understand, and are not wise, despite their ability to perform some tasks just as well as the professionals. He also says that people who rely on their senses may have authoritative knowledge of a sort, but not wisdom.
Explain why you think Aristotle says these things, and what you understand him to mean by “knowledge” and by “wisdom”—what they are and why they are good. Strive to explain his points in your own terms, but use brief quotations to convince your reader that what you say really might be Aristotle’s idea. Finally, consider whether Aristotle’s ideas of knowledge and wisdom make sense in today’s world. Is there a different idea of knowledge or wisdom that better suits our situation and experience?

In reflecting upon Aristotle‘s Being qua being, especially his demarcation of wisdom from experiential and technical knowledge, I want to set his view against the more fluid conception of knowledge proposed by Nietzsche. Aristotle places wisdom above other forms of knowledge, stating, “For the wise man must not be ordered but must order, and he must not obey another, but the less wise must obey him” (982a17-19). My argument is that Aristotle’s account of what it is to know holds up today, but his ranking does not. In many fields we now act on knowledge of the “that” without the “why”, and the kind of wisdom that suits this situation is one Aristotle himself described, practical wisdom, which he ranked below theoretical wisdom.
Experience, art, and why experience falls short
Aristotle establishes a clear hierarchy between experience, knowledge, and wisdom: while experience is valuable for practical action, it falls short of knowledge or wisdom. He notes, “With a view to action, experience seems in no respect inferior to art… But yet we think that knowledge and understanding belong to art rather than to experience…” (981a12-26). The reason is the difference between particulars and universals: “experience is knowledge of individuals, art of universals” (981a15-16). The physician does not cure “man” but Callias or Socrates (981a18-20), so the person of experience can treat the patient in front of them as well as the physician can, sometimes better. What the person of experience lacks is the general account of why the treatment works, and so they cannot teach it: “we think art more truly knowledge than experience is; for artists can teach, and men of mere experience cannot” (981b7-10).

Aristotle marks knowledge as a progression beyond experience, an understanding of the ‘why’ behind things. He states, “For men of experience know that the thing is so, but do not know why, while the others know the ‘why’ and the cause” (981a28-30). This includes both ‘technē,’ a kind of knowledge relevant to making things (craftsmanship or art), and ‘epistēmē,’ scientific knowledge. Both involve understanding the principles and causes behind facts and processes. The same test explains the line about the senses. They “give the most authoritative knowledge of particulars. But they do not tell us the ‘why’ of anything” (981b10-13): sight tells me that fire is hot, not why it is.
Wisdom, and why knowledge is good
Wisdom (Sophia), according to Aristotle, is the pinnacle in this hierarchy. He observes, “Clearly then Wisdom is knowledge about certain principles and causes” (982a1-3). Wisdom is theoretical knowledge of first principles, which is why Aristotle ranks the theoretical sciences above the productive ones (981b30-982a1) and keeps practical know-how out of it. The wise person knows the most universal causes, which are the hardest to know and the furthest from the senses, and is the one most “capable of teaching the causes” (982a12-14).
Why any of this is good is answered in the first line of the book: “All men by nature desire to know” (980a21). Knowledge satisfies a desire we already have, and wisdom satisfies it best, because it is pursued for nothing beyond itself. Men began to philosophise out of wonder, not for any use (982b12-21), and so “as the man is free, we say, who exists for his own sake and not for another’s, so we pursue this as the only free science, for it alone exists for its own sake” (982b25-28). This is also why the wise should order and not be ordered: the science that knows the end for which everything else is done is the one that directs the others (982b4-7).
Does it make sense today?

Does it make sense today?
The common objection is that technology and the accessibility of information have made deep knowledge easier to acquire, so the boundaries Aristotle draws have blurred. By his own test this does not follow. Easier access to information gives people more of the “that”, which is still experience. Reading that a drug lowers blood pressure is not knowing why it does.
A better objection is that in many fields the “that” now runs ahead of the “why”, and we act on it anyway. Surgeons have used general anaesthesia since 1846 without a settled account of how it produces unconsciousness. Machine learning models predict protein structures and write passable prose, and for almost any particular output, the people who build them cannot state its causes. Interpretability research has traced the mechanism behind some narrow behaviours, such as a model adding two numbers, but that is a few worked cases, far from the general account Aristotle would call art. By Aristotle’s test this is experience, knowledge of particulars that cannot be fully taught as principle, yet it is some of the most valuable knowledge we have. The ranking in Metaphysics I, which puts the person who knows the cause above the person who gets the result, fits these cases badly.
Nietzsche goes further. His perspectivism denies that there is a view from nowhere from which the most universal causes could be known: “There is only a perspective seeing, only a perspective ‘knowing’; and the more affects we allow to speak about one thing, the more eyes, different eyes, we can use to observe one thing, the more complete will our ‘concept’ of this thing, our ‘objectivity’, be” (On the Genealogy of Morals, III.12). As Clark (1990) argues, this is not the claim that all knowledge is merely subjective. It says objectivity comes from adding perspectives, not escaping them, which makes the experience of the practitioner a part of knowledge rather than a stage below it. Nietzsche’s criticism of a predetermined human telos, and the Übermensch who creates values rather than discovering them (Ansell-Pearson, 2012), attack Aristotle’s ethics more than this hierarchy, since sophia in Metaphysics I is theoretical knowledge, not moral knowledge.
Conclusion

Conclusion
The idea of wisdom that suits our situation is already in Aristotle, in the Nicomachean Ethics rather than the Metaphysics. Practical wisdom (phronesis) is the ability to deliberate well about particulars, and Aristotle grants that “some who do not know, and especially those who have experience, are more practical than others who know”: someone who knows that light meats are wholesome but not which meats are light will not produce health, while someone who only knows that chicken is wholesome is more likely to (NE VI.7, 1141b16-21). That is the passage this question started from, seen from the other side. Aristotle still ranked phronesis below sophia, because “man is not the best thing in the world” (1141a20-22). I would reverse the ranking. Knowing the causes remains the best account of what it is to understand something, but when the causes are unknown, as they often are now, the wisdom worth having is the experienced judgment of what to do anyway, checked against as many perspectives as we can gather.

Question 

In the Appendix to Ethics Part One (pp. 180-85), Spinoza criticizes the idea “that God directs all things to some definite end” and “that God has made all things for man and has made man to worship God.” (181)
He goes on to raise and answer three questions 1:

Why do people believe such things?
Why are these beliefs mistaken?
What is the connection between these mistaken beliefs and wrong ideas about good and evil, beauty and ugliness, and other qualities?

Using your own words, explain what Spinoza says to each of these points. Brief quotations are appropriate, but your explanation of the arguments should be in your own terms, and should be complete, that is, explaining all of his points.
In conclusion, say what if anything we can learn from this discussion. Is his point one that still needs making, or have we left the mistakes Spinoza refutes behind? Or maybe you think they are not mistakes, or that his criticism is faulty

In reading Baruch Spinoza‘s “Ethics,” particularly his repudiation of teleology and the anthropocentric conception of divine power, I contrast these views with Friedrich Nietzsche’s “Beyond Good and Evil.” Spinoza, with his staunch rationalism, argues that misconceptions about the divine lead to a skewed understanding of morality and aesthetics. For Spinoza, morality is less about adhering to external moral codes and more about aligning oneself with an understanding of God’s nature. Nietzsche shares his scepticism of conventional morality but does without God altogether. I posit that Spinoza’s point still needs making, because purpose-based explanation is a default of the human mind rather than a stage we passed through, and that our moral values should draw strength from personal conviction but also be grounded in a rational understanding of ourselves, informed by psychology and anthropology.
(1) Why people believe that nature acts for an end
The genesis of teleological beliefs, according to Spinoza, is human ignorance and the desire to seek personal advantage. He builds on two premises: “all men are born ignorant of the causes of things, and … all men want to seek their own advantage and are conscious of wanting this.” Because individuals are conscious of their desires but ignorant of what causes them, they think themselves free. Because they always act for their advantage, they explain everything by its purpose: “Why did that happen?” means “For what purpose?”, and once they have an answer they stop asking.
They then find, in themselves and around them, many things useful to them that they did not make: eyes for seeing, teeth for chewing, the sun for light, the sea for supporting fish. Since they did not provide these means themselves, they infer that someone else did, one or more rulers of nature with human freedom who arranged everything for human use. Having no information about the character of these rulers, they judge it from their own: the gods must want to be honoured, and each person invents a way of worshipping that will make God love them above everyone else. In this way the prejudice became superstition.

Since they did not provide these means themselves, they infer that someone else did, one or more rulers of nature with human freedom who arranged everything for human use. Having no information about the character of these rulers, they judge it from their own: the gods must want to be honoured, and each person invents a way of worshipping that will make God love them above everyone else. In this way the prejudice became superstition.
The inconveniences of nature, such as storms, earthquakes and diseases, should have refuted it. Instead people explained them as the gods’ anger at wrongs or at mistakes in worship, and when daily experience showed that misfortune falls on the pious and the impious alike, they placed the gods’ reasons among things beyond human grasp rather than give up the belief. Spinoza says this would have hidden the truth from humanity forever “if mathematics hadn’t shown them another standard of truth”, since mathematics is concerned not with ends but with the essential properties of figures.
(2) Why these beliefs are mistaken
Spinoza first argues that attributing purposes to nature inverts the true order of cause and effect. By assuming that events occur for a specific end, people treat what is an effect as a cause, and what comes first by nature as coming after. Spinoza also challenges the notion of divine purpose: if God acted for an end, God would want and therefore lack something, contradicting divine perfection. Saying God acted for God’s own sake does not help, because it still makes creation a means to something God lacked. He asserts that everything in nature occurs out of necessity and follows from God’s nature, not from a divine intention or goal.

He then shows how the doctrine defends itself. Its followers, instead of reducing an opponent’s view to the impossible, reduce it to ignorance. If a slate falls from a roof and kills a man, they say it fell in order to kill him. Answer that the wind was blowing and the man was walking past, and they ask why the wind blew just then and why the man was walking there just then, and they keep asking for the causes of causes “until you take refuge in the will of God, which is the haven of unacknowledged ignorance.” The same move appears when people see the structure of the human body: not knowing its causes, they are struck by “a foolish wonder” and conclude it was built by supernatural skill. Finally, anyone who looks for the natural causes of miracles is denounced as a heretic by those whom the people honour as interpreters of nature, because if ignorance is replaced by knowledge of mechanical processes, wonder goes with it, and so does their authority. Spinoza’s argument here was radical for his time, and he did not publish the Ethics in his lifetime; it appeared after his death in 1677.
(3) How these beliefs distort good and evil, beauty and ugliness
Spinoza extends his critique to human morality and aesthetics. Once people believe everything happens on their account, they judge as most important in each thing whatever is most useful to them, and call “good” what contributes to health and the worship of God. “Order” is the same mistake: we call things orderly when they are arranged so that we can easily imagine and remember them, and prefer order to confusion as if order were something in nature rather than a relation to our imagination. Beauty, ugliness, sweetness, harmony and the rest are likewise names for how objects affect our senses. They are “states of the imagination” that arise from how things affect individuals rather than from any quality of the things themselves.
Since human bodies differ, what seems good or ordered or pleasing to one person seems bad or confused or displeasing to another, which is why these judgments produce so much controversy and finally scepticism (“so many heads, so many attitudes”). Things that are understood, as in mathematics, do not divide people in this way. This also answers the objection that a perfect God would not have made a world with rot, ugliness and evil: “the perfection of things is to be judged solely from their nature and power”, not from whether they please or offend human senses.

What we can learn
Nietzsche recognised Spinoza as an ally. In a postcard to Franz Overbeck of 30 July 1881 he wrote, “I have a precursor, and what a precursor!”, and listed the doctrines they shared: Spinoza denies free will, purposes, the moral world order, the unegoistic, and evil. Nietzsche’s own version of point (3) is the line “There is no such thing as moral phenomena, but only a moral interpretation of phenomena” (Beyond Good and Evil, §108).
Where they part is in what replaces purpose. For Spinoza everything follows from the necessity of God’s nature, which can be understood. In §22 of Beyond Good and Evil, Nietzsche treats nature’s obedience to laws as an interpretation and proposes a competing reading in terms of the will to power. He allows this world a necessary, calculable course and acknowledges that his own reading is also an interpretation. Moral systems are tools by which groups exert influence over others through “herd instincts” (§202). He even turns Spinoza’s argument against Spinoza: the instinct of self-preservation is one more “superfluous teleological principle”, which “we owe to Spinoza’s inconsistency” (§13). So where Spinoza traces our value judgments to imagination and utility, Nietzsche traces them to power.

Does the point still need making? Kelemen, Rottman and Seston (2013) tested a narrower claim: whether time pressure makes people more likely to accept unwarranted purpose-based explanations. Their first study included 80 physical scientists, randomly assigned to a timed or untimed condition. Scientists given 3.2 seconds per judgment accepted a mean of 29\% of the test explanations, against 15\% without a deadline, nearly twice the rate. The result supports the authors’ proposal that purpose-based reasoning can persist despite scientific training. It gives some evidence for Spinoza’s claim that we are “inclined by nature to embrace it”. His further account of self-interest and religious authority needs a separate argument; this experiment measured judgments under a deadline.
The foolish wonder at the body also outlived him. William Paley’s Natural Theology (1802) argued from the design of the eye to a designer, the argument “intelligent design” still makes, and it was answered the way Spinoza said it should be, with efficient causes: Darwin’s natural selection (1859). The slate argument survives as “everything happens for a reason”.
This is also where the thesis about values comes back. Spinoza does not abolish “good”; in Part IV he redefines it as “what we certainly know to be useful to us” (IV, Definition 1). The judgments he criticises in the appendix go wrong because they project our advantage onto nature, not because they track our advantage. Values can draw strength from personal conviction, as Nietzsche wants, and still be checked against what psychology and anthropology tell us about what is in fact useful to beings like us. Spinoza’s mistake to avoid is the one that turns a fact about us into a fact about the world.

(1) Of course this is not the place to derive my explanations from the nature of the human mind. It will suffice here to build on two things that everyone must admit to be true: that all men are born ignorant of the causes of things, and that all men want to seek their own advantage and are conscious of wanting this.
From these premises it follows that men think themselves free, because they are conscious of their choices and their desires, are ignorant of the causes that incline them to want and to choose, and thus never give the faintest thought —even in their dreams!—to those causes. It follows also that men act always on account of a goal, specifically on account of their advantage, which they seek. Putting these two together, men are in a frame of mind from which efficient causes —that is, real causes—are almost totally absent, and which is saturated by thought about final causes, goals or ends or purposes. So the only explanations they look for are ones in terms of final causes—in asking ‘Why did that happen?’ they are asking ‘For what purpose did that happen?’—and when they have heard that they are satisfied, having nothing more to ask. But if they can’t get such explanations from others they have to turn to themselves, and to reflect on the ends by which they are usually led to do such things; so they necessarily judge the temperament of other men from their own temperament.
Furthermore, they find—both in themselves and outside themselves— many means that are very helpful in seeking their own advantage: eyes for seeing, teeth for chewing, plants and animals for food, the sun for light, the sea for supporting fish, and similarly with almost everything else whose natural causes—that is, whose efficient causes—they are not curious about. This leads them to consider all natural things as means to their own advantage. And knowing that they had found these means, not provided them for themselves, they had reason to think there was someone else who had prepared these means for human use. So they inferred that one or more rulers of nature, endowed with human freedom, had taken care of all things for them, and made all things for their (human) use.

And since they had never heard anything about the character of these rulers, they had to judge it from their own characters; so they maintained that the Gods direct everything for the use of men in order to bind men to them and be held by men in the highest honour! So it has come about that each man has thought up—on the basis of his own character—his own way of worshipping God, so that God might love him above all the rest, and direct the whole of nature according to the needs of his blind desire and insatiable greed. Thus this prejudice changed into superstition, and struck deep roots in men’s minds. This is why everyone tried so hard to understand and explain the final causes— the purposes—of all things.
But while trying to show that nature does nothing in vain (meaning: nothing that isn’t useful to men), they seem to have shown only that nature and the gods are as mad as men are! Look at how they ended up! Along with many conveniences in nature they couldn’t avoid finding many inconveniences—storms, earthquakes, diseases, etc. They hold that these happen because the gods—whom they judge on the basis of themselves—are angry with men for wronging them or making mistakes in their worship. And though their daily experience contradicted this, and though countless examples showed that conveniences and inconveniences happen indiscriminately to the pious and the impious alike, that didn’t lead them to give up their longstanding prejudice. It was easier for them to put the gods’ reasons for· this among the other unknown things whose uses they were ignorant of, thus remaining in the state of ignorance in which they had been born, than to destroy that whole construction and think up a new one.
So they maintained it as certain that the gods’ judgments far surpass man’s grasp. This alone would have caused the truth to be hidden from the human race for ever, if mathematics hadn’t shown them another standard of truth. It could do this because it isn’t involved in the final-causes muddle, because·it is concerned not with ends but only with the essential properties of figures. In addition to mathematics there have also been a few other things (I needn’t list them here) which have enabled a few men to notice these common prejudices and be led to the true knowledge of things.

(2) That is enough on what I promised in the first place, namely, to explain why men are so inclined to believe that all things act for an end. I don’t need many words to show that nature has no end set before it, and that all final causes are nothing but human fictions. I think I have already sufficiently established it, both by my explanation of the origins of this prejudice and also by the propositions by which I have shown that everything happens by a certain eternal necessity of nature and with the greatest perfection.
Still, I shall add this: this doctrine about ends turns nature completely upside down. For what is really a cause it considers as an effect, and conversely what is an effect it considers as a cause. What by nature comes first it makes follow. And finally, what is supreme and most perfect it makes imperfect.
The first two points are self-evident. Again, this doctrine takes away God’s perfection. For if God acts for the sake of an end, it must be that God wants something and therefore lacks something. And though the theologians and metaphysicians distinguish different kinds of ends, that doesn’t help them with the present difficulty. They say that God did everything for God’s own sake and not for the sake of the things God was going to create. For before the creation that they believe in they can’t find anything for the sake of which God could act— except God! And so they have to admit that God willed to make things happen as means to things that God wanted and lacked. This is self-evident.

I should also mention that the followers of this doctrine about ends, wanting to show off their cleverness in saying what things are for, have called to their aid a new form of argument: instead of reducing things to the impossible, they reduce them to ignorance! Their resorting to this shows that no other way of defending their doctrine was open to them.
For example, if a slate falls from a roof onto someone’s head and kills him, they will argue that the slate fell in order to kill the man. Here is how their argument goes: If it didn’t fall for that purpose because God wanted the man to be killed, how could so many circumstances have come together by chance? You may answer that it happened because the wind was blowing hard and the man was walking that way. But why was the wind blowing hard just then? Why was the man walking by just then? If you answer that the wind arose then because on the preceding day, while the weather was still calm, the sea began to toss, and that the man had been invited somewhere by a friend, then we will ask: Why was the sea tossing? Why was the man invited at just that time?
And on it goes! They won’t stop asking for the causes of causes until you take refuge in the will of God, which is the haven of unacknowledged ignorance.
Similarly, when they see the structure of the human body, these people are struck by a foolish wonder; and because they don’t know the causes of this elaborate structure they conclude that it is constructed not by mechanical processes but by divine or supernatural skill, and constituted as it is so that the parts won’t injure another.
So it comes about that someone who seeks the true causes of ‘miracles’ and is eager (like an educated man) to understand natural things, not (like a fool) to wonder at them, is denounced as an impious heretic by those whom the people honour as interpreters of nature and of the gods. For the denouncers know that if ignorance is taken away and replaced by real knowledge of mechanical processes, then foolish wonder is also taken away, depriving them of their only means for arguing and defending their authority. Enough of this; I now pass on to what I decided to treat here in the third place.

(3) After men convinced themselves that whatever happens does so on their account, they had to judge as most important in each thing whatever is most useful to them, and to rate as most excellent all the things by which they were most pleased. So they had to develop the notions: good, bad, order, confusion, warm, cold, beauty, ugliness, in terms of which they ‘explained’ natural things. I shall briefly discuss these here.
Whatever contributes to health and to the worship of God they have called ‘good’, and what is contrary to these they call ‘bad’. Those who don’t understand the real nature of things, and have only a pictorial grasp of them, mistake their own imaginings for intellectual thought; they really have nothing to say about things, but in their ignorance of things and of their own natures they firmly believe that there is an order in things. When a number of items are set out in such a way that when they’re presented to us through the senses we can easily imagine them—can easily depict them to ourselves— and so can easily remember them, we say that they are ‘orderly’; but if the opposite is true we say that they are ‘disorderly’ or ‘confused’.
And since the things we can easily imagine are especially pleasing to us, men prefer ‘order’ to ‘confusion’, as if order were something in nature more than a relation to our imagination! They also say that God has created all things to be orderly (thus unknowingly attributing imagination to God, unless they mean that God has disposed things so that men can easily imagine them). Perhaps they won’t be deterred—though they should be— by the fact that we find infinitely many things that far surpass our imagination, and many that confuse it on account of its weakness. But enough of this.

Perhaps they won’t be deterred—though they should be— by the fact that we find infinitely many things that far surpass our imagination, and many that confuse it on account of its weakness. But enough of this.
The other notions are also nothing but various states of the imagination; yet ignorant people consider them to be chief attributes of things. This is because, as I have already said, they believe that all things were made for their sake, and call the nature of a thing ‘good’ or ‘bad’, ‘sound’ or ‘rotten’ and ‘corrupt’, according to how it affects them. For example, if the motion the nerves receive from objects presented through the eyes is conducive to health, the objects that cause it are called ‘beautiful’; those that cause a contrary motion are called ‘ugly’. Those that move the sensory apparatus through the nose they call ‘pleasant-smelling’ or ‘stinking’; through the tongue, ‘sweet’ or ‘bitter’, ‘tasty’ or ‘tasteless’; through touch, ‘hard’ or ‘soft’, ‘rough’ or ‘smooth’, etc.; and finally those that affect us through the ears are said to produce ‘noise’, ‘sound’ or ‘harmony’. Some men have been mad enough to believe that God is pleased by harmony!
All these things show well enough that each person has judged things according to the disposition of his own brain; or rather, has accepted states of the imagination as things. So it is no wonder (I note in passing) that we find so many controversies to have arisen among men, and that they have finally given rise to scepticism. For although human bodies are alike in many ways, they still differ in very many. And for that reason what seems good to one seems bad to another; what seems ordered to one seems confused to another; what seems pleasing to one seems displeasing to another, and so on.

I pass over the other notions here, both because this is not the place to treat them at length and because everyone has experienced this variability sufficiently for himself. That is why we have such sayings as ‘So many heads, so many attitudes’, ‘Everyone is well pleased with his own opinion’, and ‘Brains differ as much as palates do’. These proverbs show well enough that men judge things according to the disposition of their brain, and imagine things rather than understanding them. For if men had understood natural things they would at least have been convinced of the truth about them, even if they weren’t all attracted by it. The example of mathematics shows this. So we see that all the notions by which ordinary people are accustomed to explain nature are only states of the imagination, and don’t indicate the nature of anything except the imagination.
Many people are accustomed to arguing in this way: If all things have followed from the necessity of God’s most perfect nature, why are there so many imperfections in nature? why are things so rotten that they stink? so ugly that they make us sick? why is there confusion, evil, and wrong-doing? I repeat that those who argue like this are easily answered. For the perfection of things is to be judged solely from their nature and power; things are not more or less perfect because they please or offend men’s senses, or because they are useful or harmful to human nature.

He crouched at the deck edge, looking down at nothing. His arms were folded, his hands clenched, his fingers curled inward as if to protect what lay beneath the skin. A coyote wailed in the distance on the ridge. The sound dwindled into silence.
He moved to his usual reading chair. His eyes followed the broad hump of the hill beyond the terraced garden.
The room behind him stayed in shadow. Only the loose white curtain stirred in the quiet wind as he turned.
The sky was still deep indigo black, but its edges had shifted into inky outlines of mountains.
A rosy glow seeped into the sky past Topanga. The last ragged night clouds lingered a moment in silhouette. A faint plume of fog uncurled above the ridge, flaring rose-gold, luminous as breath. The hills swam into half-form, breathing with him. Time still belonged to uncertainty, the dissolution of dreams. When the light came fully, it would be time to begin again.
He came back inside, into the hollow house. 
The first thing he did was breathe deeply through his nose; the scent of stale coffee filled the cold room. 
Light hush. Stillness stretched on after the abrupt birdsong, after the soft rush of the morning breeze against the wide panes.
The living room was in shadow. Only a faint orange glow from the upstairs hallway slanted across the reading nook. He settled on the sofa. Beside him lay the newspaper, fallen to the floor, creased down the middle, open in a shallow dome. 
His eye fell immediately on the bold headline. The rest of the paper held such exciting news: politics, a possible wildfire, and a new cooking show. Quiet light touched his bare feet and felt warm.
He took a cup of orange juice and an espresso. With a slight clink, he set the cup on its saucer and carried both to the back steps. He sat with the newspaper, sipped the drinks, and read it aloud. 
The phone rang once, twice. He did not hear it. Eventually he put the paper down, got up, went to the desk, turned on the computer, and sat stiffly, waiting. And waiting still…

Another click, then another message: “I’ve been trying to find a way to tell you that I think your presence is getting in the way of the space that I need in order to make the kind of romantic connection that I feel you deserve. It’s very strange and absurd, and I’m not sure I can explain it. All I know is that, at this stage in my life, I like being by myself. I want to think about who I am and how I want to live my life. That way, I can figure out the kind of relationship I need to have, and be with someone who will stay with me in my future. Right now, I can’t imagine being in a relationship that deserves the kind of attention and energy you want it to have. That being said, I don’t want you to think that I don’t value how special you are. I’d much rather see you with someone else that isn’t me.”
It was some minutes before he responded. He wondered whether they should have resolved things in some way. She clearly knew him better than he did, and maybe he should have known that what he had to offer could not satisfy what she wanted. 
But how could he have expected her to answer in kind? There were times when he could not stand being himself. He said that he was sorry he had upset her and asked her whether she wanted him to say anything else. 
She did the same, and he likewise said he had nothing more to say. He received a further ping: “Coffee next week?” He replied that coffee sounded good and smiled in the way he usually did when he smiled.
[Life moved on, and he thought to himself: “We will be okay.”]

In the context of Gartner’s hype cycle, what has been the trajectory of generative conversational AI?
Should a format including generative conversational AI be introduced to replace traditional essay assignments in educational settings,
and if so, what are some potential implications for student learning and assessment? (Dwivedi et al., 2023)

Introduction.
Historically, Alan Turing’s seminal work “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” laid the foundation for exploring the possibilities of a thinking machine (Turing, 1950).
Subsequently, the development of AI took a symbolic approach: world representations through systems that manipulate high-level symbols to arrive at a result, commonly referred to as Good Old-Fashioned AI (GOFAI) (Haugeland, 1997).
While GOFAI showed promise through rule-based reasoning, its limitations became apparent in the 1980s when the field entered an “AI Winter.” This was likely due to the cynicism within the AI researchers’ community and a reduction in funding, which halted most research and development (Hendler, 2008).
Given Moore’s Law and the exponential growth of compute and data, a new approach to AI arose, focusing on statistical methods and connectionist networks such as artificial neural networks. (Haugeland, 1997) dubbed this approach as New Fangled AI (NFAI). Fast forward to the 21^{\text{st}} century, ML has entered the mainstream through the rise of generative AI (GenAI).
This paper posits that GenAI has passed the “peak of inflated expectations” and is entering the “trough of disillusionment” on Gartner’s hype cycle. It will also examine the implications of machine-assisted interfaces beyond conversational UI and their pedagogical consequences for student learning and assessment.
Gartner’s hype cycle.
For context, applications such as ChatGPT are built on top of Transformers architecture and pre-trained on a large corpus of text (Brown et al., 2020). Given
an input sequence of tokens length n, these systems will predict the next tokens at index n+1. Most implementations of transformers are autoregressive (Croft, 2023), meaning that the model generates one token at a time, each conditioned on every token before it.
Assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, (Keles et al., 2022, p. 4) establish worst-case lower bounds for exact full self-attention and certain approximations. Under their dimension and error assumptions, these exclude running times of O(n^{2-\varepsilon}) for any fixed \varepsilon>0. Actual serving costs also depend on the model, workload, and implementation.

Gartner’s own 2024 assessment places GenAI past the peak: “GenAI is in the Trough of Disillusionment with the beginning of industry consolidation” (Gartner, 2024). Three factors drove it to the peak: rapid advancement in research, widespread enterprise adoption, and increased public awareness.
Public awareness came first. ChatGPT was released in November 2022 and was estimated to have reached 100 million monthly users two months later, faster than any consumer application before it.1
Ongoing research in GenAI, specifically language models, spans several topics, including mechanistic interpretability (Nanda, 2023), which explores the inner workings of auto-regressive models, retrieval and verification techniques aimed to improve correctness and reduce hallucinations among LLM systems (Béchard & Ayala, 2024; Dhuliawala et al., 2023),
as well as vested interests in multimodal applications of transformers (Xu et al., 2023). Anthropic’s interpretability and alignment work (Bricken et al., 2023; Elhage et al., 2022; Templeton et al., 2024), AI21’s Jamba with its hybrid Transformer-Mamba architecture (Team et al., 2024), open-weights models from Meta, and closed models such as Google’s Gemini continue to redefine what these systems are capable of.
Enterprise adoption is evident with Salesforce (Nijkamp et al., 2023), Oracle’s collaboration with Cohere, and Microsoft’s Copilot for its 365 Product Suite. However, widespread implementation doesn’t necessarily equate to immediate, measurable productivity gains. Integrating these systems effectively into enterprise workflows to deliver tangible business value takes time and effort.

The gap between the first two factors and the third is what puts GenAI in the trough: awareness and adoption ran ahead of what the systems reliably do. As the field moves through the “trough of disillusionment”, a more realistic assessment of GenAI’s capabilities will likely emerge.
Implications of machine-assisted interfaces and its pedagogical consequences for student learning and assessment.
The proliferation of conversational user interfaces (CUI) is based upon a simple heuristic of how auto-regressive models surface their internal state through generating the next tokens.
CUIs often prove frustrating when dealing with tasks requiring larger information sets. Additionally, for tasks that require frequent information retrieval (research, academic writing), CUIs are suboptimal as they compel users to maintain information in their working memory unnecessarily.
Pozdniakov proposed a framework that incorporates both application and interaction design, emphasizing manual alignment inputs from end users (Pozdniakov et al., 2024, p. 3).
Should a format like this replace the traditional essay? I argue it should be introduced alongside the essay rather than replace it. Once a student can generate a fluent essay in seconds, the finished text no longer shows what the student did, so an assignment graded only on the final text stops measuring learning. But the skills the essay trains, building an argument and judging whether a claim is supported, are the same skills a student needs to evaluate what a model produces. Introducing the format has two major implications for student learning and assessment: a shift in core competencies and a shift in what gets assessed.

With machine-assisted interfaces, students will need to develop stronger critical thinking skills to evaluate AI-generated content and formulate precise instructions.
The focus will shift towards the process of reaching desired outcomes and improving information retrieval skills. This shift aligns with the potential for machine-assisted proofs to solve novel problems, as discussed by (Tao, 2024).
These new interfaces will require instructors to adapt their evaluation methods. If the product can be generated, the process is what has to be graded: the student submits the record of their work with the model (prompts, drafts, the claims they checked and rejected) along with the final text, and defends it in a short oral discussion with the instructor. Assessment can then consider the student’s level of engagement with a given topic, and lets students work at their own pace, since the record shows how they got there.
This approach encourages a more cross-disciplinary understanding, better preparing students for continuous learning.

Question 

Read “Of Corporations, Courts, Personhood, and Morality. Business Ethics
Quarterly, 25(4), 415-431.” (Blair, 2015)
After reading this paper and in consideration of objective reality, subjective reality and legal fiction,
do you think corporations should be regarded as separate legal “persons”?
Do you agree with Prof. Thomas Donaldson’s vision of corporations as “moral” persons?
Why or why not? How does the concept of corporate “personhood” influence our
thinking about the social responsibilities of corporations?

Corporate personhood poses philosophical challenges that intersect with practical questions of morality, responsibility and social impact. While corporations have historically been granted legal personhood
to facilitate commerce and establish clear rules of operation (Blair, 2015), this legal fiction deserves examination. This essay argues that corporations should be treated as separate legal “persons” only as a practical legal framework, and opposes (Donaldson, 1984)‘s vision of treating corporations as moral agents.
Against Donaldson’s argument
Legally, corporations are treated as separate entities, allowing them to own property, enter contracts, and be liable for debts independent of their shareholders. (Blair, 2015) highlights that this legal fiction facilitates economic growth by encouraging investment and risk-taking. The objective reality is that corporations are collectives of individuals, and legal personhood is a tool for managing complex economic activities.
The subjective reality is different. Employees, customers and courts experience a corporation as an agent: we say that a company lied or cut corners, not that some of its employees did. Courts have also extended to corporations rights once reserved for people, political speech through independent spending in Citizens United v. FEC (2010) and religious exercise in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby (2014). This is where Donaldson’s case is strongest, and the question is whether the way we experience corporations should become a claim about what they are. Conflating the legal construct with moral personhood is, I will argue, a mistake.
Donaldson (1984) posits that corporations are moral agents capable of ethical reasoning and responsibility. His test has two conditions: the organisation must be able to use moral reasons in its decision-making, and its decision-making process must control not only its actions but also its policies and rules. Many corporations meet both on paper; they have codes of conduct, ethics committees and compliance rules.
Kant’s account of moral agency shows what the test leaves out. Kantian ethics require autonomous agents capable of rational decision-making and of acting from duty (Kant, 1785). A corporation’s decision procedure can process moral reasons, but every reason that enters it is some member’s reason, and there is no corporate will, separate from the people who run the procedure, that could act from duty. When we call the corporation the moral agent, responsibility moves off the people who had the reasons and onto an entity that cannot feel blame and whose punishment falls on shareholders and employees.

A corporation’s decision procedure can process moral reasons, but every reason that enters it is some member’s reason, and there is no corporate will, separate from the people who run the procedure, that could act from duty. When we call the corporation the moral agent, responsibility moves off the people who had the reasons and onto an entity that cannot feel blame and whose punishment falls on shareholders and employees.
When corporations are granted personhood, they shape the socio-political landscape, often without meaningful accountability. Chomsky (1999) argues that corporations, empowered by neo-liberal policies, often operate contrary to the public good, undermining democratic processes and social welfare. This perspective reinforces the view that corporations lack the moral orientation necessary to be considered moral persons.
The profit motive is a weaker objection than it looks. People are also constrained by self-interest and contracts, and we still treat them as moral agents. Nor does corporate law require a company to maximise profit at every turn: the business judgment rule gives directors wide discretion to weigh employees, communities and long-term reputation, although Delaware courts have rejected a board that openly put another purpose above stockholder value (eBay Domestic Holdings v. Newmark, 2010). What Donaldson’s vision fails to address is the point about the will. It attempts to impose ethical obligations on corporate behaviour by giving the corporation agency, when the obligations can only be met by the people inside it. (Blair, 2015) reaches a compatible conclusion from the legal side: the courts have treated corporations as persons for some purposes, but the law does not unequivocally support Donaldson’s vision.
Implications on social responsibility
By treating corporations as persons, we risk anthropomorphising entities that are fundamentally tools of capital accumulation. (Zuboff, 2020) describes how corporations exploit
personal data for profit, often at the expense of individual privacy and autonomy, with the rise of surveillance capitalism. Similarly, (Crawford, 2021) demonstrates
the deployment of AI to optimise corporate efficiency often lacks moral oversight, exacerbating inequalities and affecting marginalised communities disproportionately.

By recognising that corporations are not moral agents, we shift the onus onto legal frameworks and societal pressures to enforce ethical behaviour. This understanding aligns with the objective reality of corporations as collections of individuals whose actions must be guided by laws and norms rather than assumed moral capacities.
Corporate personhood should be recognised as a limited legal fiction. While legal personhood serves practical functions in commerce and law, extending this to claims of moral personhood obscures the need for external regulation and democratic oversight of corporate power. Instead of expecting corporations to embody moral principles, society should strengthen regulatory frameworks that ensure corporate actions align with the broader public interest, especially in the era of AI and data capitalism. 1

House by the railroad, Edward Hopper
The apartment was a cast-off corner of an old hosiery mill, ten paces to the windows blackened with soot and wood dust.
Gas pipes ran along the brick walls like exposed veins. A single flickering lamp cast everything in amber shadows.
Sunlight crept a cautious half-flight up the ashen brick, then gave up, leaving the upper reaches in permanent dusk.
Steel trusses crossed fifteen (no, twenty) feet overhead, bolted tight as though to contain the resonance of its past glory days.
Air tasted of coal dust and latent cold.
The radiator in the corner had been painted over so many times it looked like a small government monument to inefficiency,
its brass nameplate reading “Reg. No. 7439-B” in script so ornate it might have been lifted from a Victorian death certificate.
The galley kitchenette clung to the south wall: single hotplate, half-sized fridge, enamel sink no wider than his shoulders.
The Turkish cezve sat cold on the burner. J had brought it from the Berkeley flea market, back when mornings meant something.
“For our mornings,” she’d said, and he’d believed in plural futures then.
Across the room, the futon disappeared beneath drifts of half-folded laundry.
He sat at the blond-wood desk that N had helped him carry up the stairs last winter, or was it the winter before?
The MacBook’s A and W keys had been rubbed to ghosts by his index finger.
Eight coffee cups formed a semicircle around the laptop.
One, two, three… six, six, seven, eight… ten… seventeen. He counted between the flickers.
“Vereinbarung”. Page sixty-three. Agreement. Arrangement. Understanding. He typed: “contract”.
…
The cursor hadn’t moved for another twenty minutes.

Ausführungsbestimmungen. Executive provisions. Or maybe just decisions. Or maybe nothing at all.
It was Tuesday, which meant he should have been on bar shift four hours ago. Or was it Thursday?
The phone showed sixteen missed calls: K from Casa’s, the coffee shop manager.
Phone buzzing:
(415) Calling…
Her area code.
He let it ring. Watched the screen go black.
He deleted the other voice mails without listening.
The radiator clanged through what daylight remained.
His hands shook as he reached for the chipped Carrara-white mug. The espresso had grown a skin.
The coffee tasted like yesterday.
Across the courtyard, the couple in 3B had their curtains half-drawn again. Her blouse gaped; his hands braced against brick.
Sweat on her collarbone. He looked away, then back.
He tongued the roof of his mouth: The chalky residue was now gone. Soon.
A knock at the door. People had been knocking all week: the landlord’s notices, gas inspections, the property manager about his succulents dying on the fire escape. Or was that last week? Time kinked around the pills.

  “It’s T. From the shop.”
Which morning? The one that stretched back in time, or forward into the one that may never come?
Laptop showed 3:47 PM Tuesday. His watch: 8:15. The cezve was still cold. The grounds in the pot were dry, still.
He stood, knees buckled. When had he last stood? Ninety-seven pages complete. The floor tilted, then leveled. He counted the coffee bags on the counter: seventeen,
half torn, the other spilled on top of the counter. He couldn’t remember emptying them.

“I know you’re in there man. I can smell the coffee.”
But the cezve was cold. He smelled his palms. They reeked of stale espresso.
  “I’m sick,” he rasped.
    “Yeah, okay. Just… K wants to know if you’re coming back. Ever.”
He patted his pockets. One bar left. The pharmacy on King closed at six. His hand shook against the brick wall.
  “Tell him Thursday.”
    “It is Thursday.”
  “NEXT THURSDAY!” he shouted, voice splintering.
Footsteps receded.
    “Okay, just checking. You okay, bud?”
    He stared at the cezve. Still cold. J’s mornings were two thousand miles away.
    “Ye—s,” he murmured.
The hallway fell silent. He saved the file FINAL_FINAL_V7.txt, and opened his notebook: “Translation as a disappearing act.”
New e-mail from ktiindustries@kti.de: “Standard rate, due upon completion.”
He dry-swallowed the last half-bar.
Thought-threads arranged themselves into neat ledger rows. Outside, light drained through budding branches.
His phone rang: San Francisco again, Dr. M’s office about the missed appointment.
Radiator knocked once, twice. A brown leaf pirouetted off the last living plant and lay on the sill. Tomorrow he would water them. Or Thursday.
He stood, eye fixed blankly on the door. T’s footsteps had faded, but the knocking persisted inside his skull. That clanging noise, that buzz. His jaw tensed, and he wiped the damp palms against the jeans.
The tremors had returned, fingers twitching.
The pharmacy closes at six.
He fumbled for his wallet, fingers shaking as he counted the bills: twenty, forty, sixty. Expired credit card, edges worn. Barely enough for two bars.
At the door, he paused and looked back at the apartment: the cold cezve, the blinking cursor, the untranslated paragraph.
  “Two thousand miles…” he murmured.

perception of a partner
Aristotle calls a friend “another self.” The Magna Moralia, which carries his name, adds the image of a mirror,1 because a virtuous friend can help us see our own character. A partner remains another human being carrying their own account of the relationship.
They are the ones that made “rupture and repair”2 possible: someone to cry, disappoint, or annoy and still continue with. The relationship wouldn’t fracture at the first conflict.
A partner is someone whose flaws become “your whole life”: their quirks become woven into your daily life.
They have you “tossing and turning throughout the night”: their presence in your life has become significant enough to disturb your equilibrium. They’re Ava’s “pea on the bottom of the mattress”3 that makes you unable to rest easily in old patterns.
A partner and you borrow time from each other without knowing how long you have. That uncertainty makes the time precious.
A partner is someone you choose to keep learning with. When one arrangement stops working, you can try another. As Ava puts it, no one “can predict all the challenges that will emerge over 20 years of loving someone.”
The partner is both witness and accomplice to your life’s narrative, though they may be writing a completely different story in their own mind. It’s this disconnect, the impossible attempt to fully know another consciousness while trapped in our own, that makes partnership both necessary and perpetually incomplete.

Kipling’s archaisms are there to give this document a 17th-century weight which it does not actually have: he composed it in 1922, at H. E. T. Haultain’s request, three years before the first ceremony. The ceremony remains semi-secret, open only to engineers and engineers-to-be. The communitas wrought by this in the room is real enough but can best be characterized as a feeling. Emotivism, then, lies close at hand: feelings are what emotivism is most interested in.

Remains after the southern span fell in 1907, killing 75.
The clause I keep returning to is or be privy to the passing of. In 1907 the chords of the Quebec Bridge were visibly bending, the consulting engineer in New York was told, and his telegram to stop loading the span was still being discussed when it fell.
And there’s the phenomenology of a ring actually being worn. The thing itself is nothing to write home about: it is not a ring that makes a remarkable impression on the hand it adorns. The distinctive sound of its click onto my table begins to disappear. After about four months of wear, the iron ring is just another piece of jewelry in a ring box, and the half-amused tap I give it each morning when I put it on is just another doodle on a napkin.
The whole affair is meant to have a certain effect, namely, to nudge me into a gradually deepening self-consciousness about the ethical nature of things. Moral utterances are ultimately expressions of attitude; they cannot be reduced without loss to statements of fact (as Ayer and Stevenson long ago insisted). I wanted to conclude from this that the scheme fails, that no sound on a piece of jewelry is going to shift my moral sensibilities. The inference runs the other way. If moral language is attitude, then ritual and repetition are exactly the things that shift it, and Stevenson’s whole account of ethical words is about their pull on other people’s attitudes.1
What the ceremony really does is create a sudden warm sense of tribal belonging: murmured sentiments, punctilious recitations, the performance of communal grammatical forms. Particularly when the archaic words are followed by the Obligation’s punchy line, it produces the happy feeling of belonging to something bigger than oneself. The ethical core of what’s being achieved is in the shared feeling the recitations produce, the feeling of belonging to a community. In the language game of the engineering profession, the ethical sense relies on blik, Hare⁠’s name for that definite though unfounded sense of how things really are.

I am aware now, past the midpoint in the first post-graduate summer, that after five years the word student has begun to fall away from me as the default position from which to run meaning off my actions. It’s one thing to drop the title ‘student’; it’s something else that the roles that go with it, the other people in similar sets of clothes, the tiny rituals and screams and class distinctions that make all the difference to how we live, should be quietly dissolved when the course actually ends. It’s odd to miss Exam Week now, even in memory. It is odd, too, to recognize that one’s convivial relationships with fellow students in university were primarily sustained by shared obligations, and that those obligations served with delicate economy as the fragile scaffold of a communal life.
But this feeling of oddness is nothing compared to that of my luggage on the GO train to Hamilton the morning of the ceremony itself, riding past the trees and fields and the glittering lakes and rivers. Convocation serves as a ready-made narrative symbolisation, a figuration of closure. It has no bearing on reality.
The ceremony attempts to generate meaning in the here-and-now practices of the institution through commitment to a rule-governed form of life. In Wittgenstein’s words:

If I have exhausted the justifications I have reached bedrock, and my spade is turned. Then I am inclined to say: ‘This is simply what I do.’ (Wittgenstein, 1953)

If I have exhausted the justifications I have reached bedrock, and my spade is turned. Then I am inclined to say: ‘This is simply what I do.’ (Wittgenstein, 1953)

This seems a reasonable way to describe graduation. University education is nothing if not an immersion in many and varied language games, engineering for one thing, but also ethics, and aesthetics, and social rituals of all sorts, each of which has its particular rules governing how we speak and act among others. The point is that we learn to speak and act according to these rules, not that we ever succeed in justifying them.
I lost sight of the ring on my hand for a month. Much to my surprise, much to my own inexplicable relief, what endured was a quiet feeling that something is wrong about not seeing it: a connection not only with an obligation I must not forget but with a tribe and its practices, the form of life that made the notion of obligation intelligible to me in the first place.
Thus I hold my ring out in front of me. It is not quite clean, because I haven’t had much time to clean it; and it is not quite what I thought I would be holding in my hand when I finally looked back at myself and my life to this point, but then again it is.

This is the first in a series on relationships.
The first part is an exploration into Jung’s archetypes and how love is a mutual becoming.

Environs du cap Misène (1904)
I’ve been mulling over this all morning, wondering what I want to write about love: romantic, platonic, familial.
What do I really know about it? Less than I’d like, more than I admit.
I went to grab a coffee earlier today. The barista knows my order by now: Latte, oat milk, hot.
Today she slides over not just my drink but a small envelope, worn at the edges like it’s been carried around for a while. Her eyes meet mine for just a moment longer than usual:
“Someone left this for you,” she says, then turns to the next customer.
Inside, three words in unfamiliar handwriting:
Love is coming.
I stand there, coffee cooling, envelope light in my hands. Part of me wants to ask who left it, when, why. The other part understands that some gifts are meant to stay mysteries.
I pocket the note. Outside, February wind cuts through my jacket. But I’m thinking about how strange it is, how a few words from an unknown hand can make a person feel less, alone in the times of a loneliness epidemic.

From childhood through adulthood, we are drawn into relationships to be loved, and also to feel that we are part of something greater than ourselves.
This connection is often mistaken for the desire for another person’s affection,
when it is a yearning for a sense of home: a state of being where one is seen and accepted.
The notion that love is about belonging challenges the popular narrative that it is a transaction or a fleeting emotional high.
It reframes our loneliness:
isolation stems from a disconnection from the fact that we belong, more than from a lack of love.
a projection of the Anima/Animus
Jungian psychology posits that romantic attraction begins with the projection of the anima (the unconscious feminine aspect in men) or animus (the unconscious masculine aspect in women) onto another person.
This projection creates the illusion of “completeness,” as the beloved becomes a vessel for unintegrated parts of the self. For example, a man might idealise a partner as the embodiment of nurturing sensitivity (qualities he has repressed in his conscious identity), while a woman might project assertiveness or intellectual rigor onto a partner, mirroring her latent animus.
Where love reigns, there is no will to power; and where the will to power is paramount, love is lacking. The one is the shadow of the other.Carl Jung, On the Psychology of the Unconscious, CW 7, §78
However, such projections are inherently unstable. When relationships falter under the weight of unmet archetypal expectations, the disillusioned ego often retreats into shame or resentment,
mistaking the collapse of projection for the failure of love itself.
defensive isolation, and its shadows
Heartbreak ruptures the psyche’s fragile equilibrium, triggering an encounter with the shadow,
the repository of rejected traits and unresolved traumas. To avoid confronting this darkness, individuals often erect psychological barriers.
These walls manifest as emotional detachment, intellectualisation of intimacy, or compulsive self-reliance, all attempts to “protect” the ego from further annihilation.
For instance, an individual going through post-divorce isolation 1 or an individual dealing with limerence illustrate how the shadow’s fear of vulnerability fuels self-sabotage. As someone on r/Jung put the terror of psychic disintegration:
The body will not allow itself to be exposed to annihilation. It’s prepared to annihilate itself to avoid thatr/Jung, reddit

Yet these walls, while temporarily numbing pain, perpetuate a cycle of alienation. By refusing to engage with the shadow’s raw material (grief, rage, longing), the individual stagnates, mistaking the atrophy of emotional risk for “strength”.
Jung viewed heartbreak as an initiatory ordeal, compelling the ego to confront its limitations and renegotiate its relationship with the Self.
The key lies in holding the tension between love’s idealised projections and its messy realities.
Alain de Botton’s assertion that love is a fundamental human requirement stems from his analysis of existential loneliness, “the tax we pay for consciousness”.
The anguish of feeling “out of love” arises from a misalignment between our idealised projections of connection and the reality of relationship.
Romanticism, he argues, sold humanity a dangerous myth: that a soulmate could resolve this existential solitude. When reality fails to meet this ideal, as it
invariably does, many retreat into emotional isolation, interpreting disillusionment as proof of love’s impossibility rather than its maturation.
What must endure isn't "love" but friendship and trust.
Jungian love implies love as an antidote to modernity’s existential despair. Here, love becomes a rebellion against nihilism through daily acts of attention: the way a hand adjusts to another’s in the dark, or the pause before voicing a difficult truth.
Alain Badiou warns against algorithmic dating (and in In Praise of Love, 2009) as a way of sanitising love of risk, which sterilises its transformative potential.
The surge in “spiritual but not religious” affiliations reflects a hunger for transcendent meaning, a void that Jungian belonging fills through archetypal narratives and secular rituals fill through shared meals. Both reject individualism’s isolation: love is the quiet revolution of mutual becoming.
